utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Baccard. The cross-examination by Mr. Ivetic will now continue. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, Doctor. Thank you again for your time and I will try to finish this as briefly as possible since I only have two more topics to finish with you. Yesterday we finished up with the Izbica site and now I would like to move to another local quickly in Kacanik. And just to confirm a couple of things to make sure I'm reading the reports right. With respect to the autopsies performed at Kotlina, am I correct that they were conducted -- that these autopsies were rather brief and were undertaken in less than desirable circumstances at the Kacanik cemetery which is some distance away from the site where the bodies were excavated?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't use those words. The post mortem examination were restricted because of the condition in which we found the bodies. These were largely degraded because of the wounds and the putrefaction processes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. You've answered my second question as well. I'm going to have to slow down though because the interpreters have asked me to slow down so I will have to comply. Now, Doctor, with respect to the artefacts that were recovered with these remains that were excavated from the well in Kotlina, am I correct that several of the sets of remains had leather all-terrain boots on their feet?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take part in the post mortem examination conducted at Kotlina, so I personally did recover no boots. And as far as this detail is concerned, it is not in my -- contained in my summary report. You need to refer to the report by Drs. Markwalder and Daniel Wyler.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know since we talked a little bit about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you know if the report by these two doctors contains information about the boots?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It does contain information about boots. I was trying to figure out if the -- what -- if he had any more information about these boots. P361 at page 24, for instance, describes "all-terrain" which I'm not sure what that means in terms of describing the leather boots that were on one of the bodies and there were I believe a total of six bodies that had some sort of leather boots. So I was wondering, in his discussions with the team, if he had any additional information on that. If he doesn't, I'm prepared to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not meet the members of the team because I was only working on the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. Then one more thing, if you know. We talked a bit about ballistics and shells yesterday. Do you have any information to add on to the -- what's already specified in the report -- in the Austrian report at page 75 regarding the discovery of Chinese-manufactured bullet casings at the scene in Kotlina in addition to 7.62-calibre bullets of Yugoslav origin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a reference to that part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: P361, page 75. I believe it identifies Chinese munitions from a particular factory manufactured in 1964 is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, Doctor, if you know. If you don't know, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, let me remind you that I'm a forensic pathologist. I'm not an ammunitions and weapons expert, and therefore I have not included this detail in my summary report. I just focussed on the percentage figures, causes of death. Those reports stated that 84 per cent of the victims had died due to the effects of an explosion, whereas 12 per cent had died through bullet wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just for clarification, the reference I have here and which is what I saw yesterday is that it is not cartridge casings but a singular cartridge case out of many that were found at the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm being refreshed by the ... [French on English translation] I'm getting some kind of translation of my own words. I'm seeing now that the last sentence that talks about cartridges may refer in general to all of the 12 that were found including the one that was the Chinese make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the last area on Kotlina, before we move on to my last area, there were -- am I correct that there were I believe two or three corpses -- I believe it was three corpses recovered from the cemetery near the mosque in Kotlina as opposed to the well?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three bodies according to the identification contained in the report drafted by my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when talking about these corpses recovered from the mosque, I'm assuming that no conclusions could be reached about the location where these individuals had expired. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: This did not appear in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, I'd like to move to Krusha e Vogel or Mala Krusa which is another area you covered in your report, but before I do, I would like to cover some points about the extent and limitations of forensics investigations since I've been reading up on some literature offered by some of your colleagues including John Clark and an anthropologist Dr. Susan Black who actually did the Mala Krusa investigations and I want to make sure that I'm on the same page and that I'm understanding the basic principles correctly. Now, my understanding - and I'm asking you if you would agree with this - is that in normal pathology practice, deciding whether an injury has occurred in life as opposed to post mortem is determined by looking at things such as bruising, swelling, and bleeding and that while this is very difficult in decomposed bodies, in skeletonised remains it is nearly impossible.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not quite correct. On a microscopic examination, on the edge of a fracture, you can distinguish blood residues and blood infiltration, but as a rule, it is on soft tissue that this is easier to highlight this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, if we can move to Mala Krusa and the findings of the team from Glasgow that you reviewed. According to I believe both Dr. Black's report and yours there was only one set of remains, that is to say, remains from one individual recovered from this site, from this village, that showed signs of cremation and that the others are said to have no indications of cremation. Now what I want to ask you is, based upon that, can we conclusively exclude to a degree of reasonable scientific certainty the possibility that any of these other remains were subjected to fire; that is to say, if they do not show signs of cremation, can we exclude the possibility that the remains were exposed to fire?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the report provided by Professor Vanezis and Professor Black, as far as I'm concerned, I did indicate that these human remains included four different individuals and that signs of burning related to the four bodies but these reports would be better displayed on the screen and therefore I could check this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at P110, the first page should suffice, since they were nice enough to do a summary of all the remains recovered from the three locations on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we can perhaps assist the doctor and finish the examination since this is my last area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I don't believe that we have -- I don't believe that we have a French version of this exhibit. We have the English there on the left. Is that something that we can use to assist to refresh your recollection? And I think the part you're probably going to be interested in is the part under the heading remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think -- my learned friend might have been misled by the notification and I don't think I used this particular document in the examination-in-chief. This document, as can be seen, is dated the 29th of October, 1999, whereas at page 32, Dr. Baccard's report in respect to Mala Krusa is listed a report by Dr. Black of the 27th of October, 1999. The document placed on notification was placed in error and that is why in the examination-in-chief we referred to another document which is P2748.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 32 indicates that the examinations were carried out on the 23rd of June. Now, you tell us the date the report was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the supporting documents immediately above that, Dr. Baccard says: "This report is based on the following documents, the report of Dr. Peter Vanezis of Glasgow, regius professor of forensic medicine," et cetera. And the report of Dr. Susan Black, consultant on forensic pathology et cetera, and it's dated the 27th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what does the document we are looking at now relate to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document we are looking at relates to another examination that both of them did but it is not in the indictment, another examination in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was it also at Krusha e Vogel?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. The document in relation to the indictment in relation to Dr. Baccard's report is as I indicated Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there must be two. There's one by Vanezis and one by Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm looking for right now, Your Honours, since I don't think I had that on the notification. Does counsel have a number for that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The forensic pathologist, Dr. Vanezis, and the forensic pathologist, Dr. Black, brought together Exhibit 2748 is a combined report. The part signed by Dr. Vanezis is of the 10th of November, 1999, as indicated by Dr. Baccard and that signed by Dr. Black is the 27th of October, 1999, also as indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's P2748?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Herein lies my confusion, Your Honour. That report relates to Krusha e Vogel, Velika Krusa, Krusha e Madhe, Velika Krusa, not Krusha e Vogel. So therein is my confusion. I thought we were talking about Mala Krusa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, your point -- your point may be equally valid because if what you're after is evidence of the absence of --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- burning injuries, then you're getting it from the document you're relying on. And so far it would appear that the one the Prosecution are relying on doesn't relate to the locus you're concerned about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hope so. I hope there's not another document that I don't know about that I should have had to prepare. I think I can still ask the two questions I had in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, there does seem to be an issue here over the locality that we are concerned about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These are sister villages. My understanding effectively it's the same place Mala Krusa in -- Krusha e Vogel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but if you put on the screen 2748, the one you've just identified. Can we see it, please. Velika Krusa is a different village from Krusha e Vogel. I think that means old Krusa but...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It means greater or large, big Krusa and small Krusa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Small Krusa. Can you remind me, Mr. Ivetic, of the paragraph in --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The doctor's report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph 75 of the indictment that deals with these villages?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, there are two separate incidents alleged, one in Velika Krusa one in Mala Krusa. It's my understanding these villages are apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- identify the paragraph in -- it must be in 75 somewhere --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Since they are both in the same municipality but they are by no means the same village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: (C), I think, Your Honour. But I don't have a copy in front of me. I'm working off memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. So it would appear that the bodies with burning injuries may not be connected to the principal incident that's referred to in that paragraph, which is the shooting and burning event in the barn, I think, that we've heard quite an amount of evidence about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and the confusion that I think -- due to the fact that at page 32 of the witness's report the heading is Krusha e Vogel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that would be Mala Krusa. And it looks now, as I'm reading through the 2748, it looks like the description of the remains is actually from Velika Krusa, so that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, let's see. Dr. Baccard, can you clarify this at all for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is important to understand that when I prepared the report, I worked on the basis of documents that had been made available to me and the information that was provided to me. And I was told that these documents concerned Krusha e Vogel. I don't know the geography of Kosovo at all, so this is why I have included this name with the corresponding reference, which you have on your screen VK0002. So I see here that it says Velika Krusa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it sounds to me as though this is something that is going to have to be resolved in the wash in due course. It may be that you've no further questions on this. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I would still like to ask questions if he can review the first page of P110 and tell me if what I'm proposing is accurate -- if my reading of this document is accurate, since it is a forensic report, he has experience in it, and he's based his findings on reviews of reports conducted by these same individuals, I think he should be able to give us at least an indication on that one area, i.e. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Stamp, you want to say something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was just going to indicate that we will provide the nexus between these bodies -- we will bring evidence to provide the nexus between these bodies and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. So you want P110 on the screen do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. I think that was -- yes, P110, it was on briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, if you could review again the summary which is on the first page. It talks about sites A, B, and C, and there they have descriptions of the remains that were recovered and I'll give you a moment or -- as long as you need to read that section. And then I just want to ask you one question relative to that.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask you to confirm that this document which is on the screen was not part of the documents that were given to me. Is that right? A priori, this is not part of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is the understanding we've come to now in discussions that we've had. It looks as if this is not in your report, although it is Krusha e Vogel, the location that is listed in your -- that is listed in the heading of your report, although I think we've now agreed that your report actually deals with Krusha e Madhe, or Velika Krusa.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you possibly scroll down, please. I've finished reading this part of the document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The question, Doctor, is based on these findings by Dr. Sue Black. Can we exclude the possibility -- strike that. Let me start again. With respect to the bulk of the bodies here, where it says that there were no evidence of cremation, with respect to the bodies that say that there was no evidence of cremation, can we exclude to a reasonable degree of scientific certainty the possibility that these remains were exposed to fire?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you focus the document or could we see the middle part here. According to what I see here - this is the first time I see this document today. Three sites are mentioned, three sites where human remains were recovered. And these human remains were commingled. They belonged to several people. As far as site A is concerned and the PGZ sample 1 SR, there were no signs of cremation and seemingly, only one person was mentioned in Sue Black's report as far as site A and PG 10 SR is concerned, I can read that this sample contained a minimum of three individuals but, more likely, six people. There were no signs of cremation on the second sample. As far as the third sample is concerned, still on site A, PGZ 15 SR, there were signs of cremation, and this -- these were signs on one person only. As far as site B is concerned Sue Black mentions two samples here. It is difficult to understand whether a skeletal inventory was possible. This is not mentioned in the report, and there are no signs of cremation here. As far as site C is concerned, only one sample was recovered and, here again, no mention -- it is not stated how many people were included in the sample and whether there was -- and no -- nothing is said about signs of cremation in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when there are no signs of cremation, can we then exclude that the remains were exposed to fire? That is to say, if remains are exposed to fire, will there always be signs of cremation?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cremation can be stronger or weaker. It depends on how close to the fire the victim has stood or -- but to give you a general answer, we -- from what I understand, here we have samples of skeletonised bones where the soft tissues exposed to fire, where soft tissue burnt. I have no -- nothing here that allows me to say it, but as far as the bones themselves that are protected by soft tissues on the fresh body, the anthropologist has noticed nothing --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for PGZ 15 SR.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to clear up, then. With respect to all the reports you looked at, am I correct that you have not looked at any reports related to Krusha e Vogel apart from the one that we have now determined deals with Velika Krusa?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list of the reports I have reviewed is to be found in my own summary report, and apparently, there was some confusion with respect to Krusha e Vogel, but this is something, information that was given me orally when I was drafting the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I guess my last question: This information was given orally to you by the doctors that did the report or by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the investigators who gave me the reports. I was not in contact with the physicians, with the doctors, who authored these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you, Doctor, you've cleared it up for me. I apologise for the confusion and for the length of my examination. I meant it to be much shorter than it was. Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can share with us the light that you've seen at the end of this, when you say that it's been cleared up for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That Krusha e Vogel that is referenced in this report is not Krusha e Vogel, that it's Krusha e Madhe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When were you given that information, Dr. Baccard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it was at the end of 2001 at the time when I was preparing my report. I was told that it was -- they were the same -- one and the same locality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you say, Mr. Stamp, that you can produce something which will clarify this, make the proper link?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Doctor, you were asked a series of questions about the post mortem examinations for the victims that were found in the well at Cirez, eight victims, and it was suggested perhaps that there was no evidence that they died from drowning, that the drowning was ante mortem. And you were asked about the basis for the finding that the drowning was ante mortem. I would like you to look at the report of the forensic pathologist who examined those bodies. I have a copy of it in French. This is Exhibit P383, which I would like to be brought up. But I would like to hand the doctor a copy of the French version. What I'm going to ask you first, Doctor, is to look to see if there is evidence on which the forensic pathologist could conclude that there was ante mortem drowning, and then I'll ask you a specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While the doctor is looking at the original French version, I could indicate to the Court that the English version does not have the photographs which are in the French version. So -- but there's a description of what's in the photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to give a very clear answer to your question and I believe that my colleagues based their diagnosis of drowning by immersion on one element, and that's the aspect of the lungs. Because you can -- there was an edema in the lungs that was -- that was caused by the drowning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you finish your explanation, could we just have a look at the relevant page. It's page 4 in the English translation. Could we scroll down a little bit. Could we scroll down to under the heading "Autopsy." Is that page 4? Is this Exhibit 383? I'm sorry. I have the page number incorrect. I think we are looking for page number with ERN 5 -- ending 5686. And that is page 56, actually, in the -- in e-court, and we have it here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This, Doctor, we can see from the report, is to some degree typical of all the victims that there are no signs of damage to vital organs likely to fit apart from what is described as signs of pneumothorax in the lungs, and that is typical of all the victims. Is that correct or can you explain what you see here?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you -- we please scroll up the page because I would like to see what body this particular report or part of the report refers to. I see, we have body S1P1C1. Can we scroll down again, please. I would like to see what is said about the lungs. There is a mistake in translation because here we -- because the pulmonary edema has been translated in English instead of a pneumothorax. It's not the same thing at all. A pulmonary edema is when serum, serosity goes into the lungs, into the alveoles because of drowning, except here we have signs of pneumothorax. And pneumothorax means that you have air that goes between the chest cavity and the lungs. It is something completely different. It has nothing to do with what you find in the original French reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So the translation to pneumothorax is incorrect. What is the correct translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've been given it, pulmonary edema.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you one question on this. Is this not a particularly unfortunate mistranslation? Because I take it that pneumothorax could be caused by a fracture of a rib.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you -- apparently you have good knowledge of medicine apparently, but here we see that there is a mention of pneumothorax. It can be a complication you find after a rib is fractured, but this does not appear in the original French reports. There is no mention of pneumothorax in the French report. You're talking about two things that are completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it might explain why counsel, who are relying on an English version, could think that there is a possible challenge to the view that -- or the opinion that the body was -- the deceased died through drowning; however, you've clarified the point for us because the report was originally written in French. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think you said, just to be sure, that pulmonary edema, as indicated in the original report, is a symptom or a sign of drowning?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. From the photographs that accompany the report, in respect to the two victims that were allegedly raped, were there attempts to indicate the signs of blood on the vulvar opening and the abrasions to the inside of the thigh in those reports or in that report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, for S1P1C1 and S1P1C2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move to Izbica, I just have one question. From the medical reports that you have, the forensic pathologist reports that you have, would you or would you not be in a position to comment on how the bodies were moved and when -- if when -- if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I thought Izbica was a site where there were no bodies that were actually recovered so I'm a little -- I just want to make sure we're talking about the same site before I can know whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Izbica is where the video relates to, where the 127 or 130 -- there was 129 or 137 bodies that were apparently exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 101. 127 were on the video, Your Honour. The only exhumation we know about was 101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the video is what I think Mr. Stamp is dealing with. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From the video you would not be in a position to comment on how, when, and where, and did -- the distance the bodies were moved, if they were moved?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. As I said previously, there are limits to the conclusions you can draw from these photographs and this video. The only obvious thing that you could note, that was some of the victims had been turned over because some of the victims were face down and their bodies had been turned over and they were lying on their back. And there were some dermabrasions on limited surfaces of some of the bodies. Dermabrasion, it means that there is excoriation, superficial excoriation on the skin and that meant that the body -- the face had been bruised by the soil, by the ground, but it was impossible to know exactly along what distance these bodies had been moved. And that was the only thing that could be said about these bodies and their movements. The only thing you could say for sure was that some of these bodies had been turned over.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Nothing further, Dr. Baccard. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, there are one or two matters perhaps relating to exhibits here. I've a note and I've now forgotten why I have this note about an appropriate application being submitted to identify six bodies from Izbica. Is that something you mentioned yesterday or is it something that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- that didn't arise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, one of the things that arose in the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yugoslav authorities relating to Izbica. And I think that it was following that in the transcript I picked up some undertaking or indication that an attempt would be made to identify six additional victims. However, that's not something that you are familiar with, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't think the situation has somewhat advanced since the Milosevic case because during this case we proffered documents to Tomasevic who put in a number of reports in respect to those bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Some, I think, with identifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the other thing is that in your list of exhibits used in this case we saw a document by a policeman from the metropolitan police in London relating to what he had discovered about the identity of victims. The one we saw may have related to Bela Crkva. Is that the only one, the only document of that nature?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, in respect to other sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My understanding is that similar documents were tendered from some of the crime-base witnesses are documents identifying the people who were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are there any documents of that nature in this --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In most of the autopsies, the persons are identified at the autopsy and the doctors who performed the autopsy indicate the base of the identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that particular one, which may be an example of others, is referred to in this list as an exhumation report issued by the metropolitan police, but when we saw it, what it was was a statement by a policeman of things that had been told to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was -- the exhumation -- what is described as an exhumation report is composed of statements of photographers, hundreds of photographs, the statement of those police officers -- two police officers involved in the identification of the bodies, and the reports of the doctors who performed the autopsies on the body or body fragments that were exhumed. So the expression "exhumation report" covers a composite set of materials involved in the whole exhumation process itself, from photographs of the terrain to the actual disinterment of the bodies to the identification of the bodies, the photograph of the bodies and the post mortem examinations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we take it that the counsel for the accused are satisfied that this supporting material relied upon by the Prosecution as being the basis for Dr. Baccard's summary is presented in a satisfactory form? It's obviously hearsay as he presents it, but the written material, no doubt, would not change in its content if we insisted on other formalities being applied to it. But, for example, where there's a document that's a statement rather than a report, there's a process, a procedure, for admitting that if it's contentious. But I wonder if we've sensed the situation correctly, that everyone's content that this material is presented in this form and that the real issue in the end of the day will be the weight to be given to it, bearing in mind that Dr. Baccard has a limited personal knowledge of the nature of the inquiries carried out by other professionals in a variety of disciplines. Now, I'm regarding the silence in response to that as a confirmation that we're proceeding along the correct lines and that we do not need to take an unduly formalistic approach to this. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have another concern tied to that. Now I really don't know what exhibits the Prosecution is tendering and what exhibits I need to work with Mr. Stamp on to come with a redacted form since the one that I thought we had was 110 and I was advised that that one is not coming in. So I think I need to know from Mr. Stamp which ones on the witness notification are being sought to be tendered with this witness before -- it won't change my answer to Your Honour's question but it will be interesting for me to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've got until tomorrow to sort that out as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You and Mr. Stamp are to meet to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We had assumed from that that you, having challenged a limited number of the documents, that you were accepting for the purposes of, I think, a very reasonable approach by the Defence to this issue, that the way in which this was being done was an order. In the Milosevic trial, I don't think any attention was paid to the formalities of presenting evidence of this nature. On the other hand, that may have been because there was a measure of realism or it may have been - and possibly more likely - because he wasn't legally represented and there was a measure of -- well, there was a limit to which the amici would take up issues. It's not clear that they would necessarily have considered an issue like this. Maybe they did and I'm being unfair to them in suggesting that it was simply a question of realism. But we don't want to leave this unsaid because we really feel that we should not have to be exploring technical difficulties about evidence of this nature and we should be able to get straight to the meat of it and the weight of it, which we see as a very debatable subject. Now, can I take it, Mr. Ivetic, that between today and tomorrow you and Mr. Stamp will sort out which of these documents have not to be considered and insofar as there is no issue between you, that we should proceed simply to give them the appropriate weight in our deliberations?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I definitely will meet with Mr. Stamp and accomplish that. I had planned to do that as soon as we finish this witness, on my side, going through and presenting highlighted versions of the exhibits with the material that I thought needed to be excluded and we were going to start that process and hopefully complete it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Insofar as you can't reach agreement, we will obviously have to be involved in adjudicating.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. The indication I've gotten so far is that we should be able to reach some agreement I think on most if not all the matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dr. Baccard, we thank you for coming to give evidence again to the Tribunal. That completes your evidence. We appreciate the limitations upon your understanding and knowledge of all the work that was done underlying these various sites and the rather unsatisfactory state in which you may feel from time to time the evidence is left orally, but you can rest assured that we will be giving close attention to all the underlying material. And in this case, where there are six accused, all separately represented, that we will have submissions, no doubt, about the weight to be attached to the various conclusions reached. So I think we have a long way to go in considering the material that you have presented to us, and we are grateful to you for the assistance you've been able to give in dealing with counsels' questions. You're now free to leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is Dr. Patrick Ball.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Ball.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do you do, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Ball.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we start by you telling us your full name, your occupation, and your present job.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Patrick Ball. I'm a sociologist and a statistician. I'm currently the director of the human rights programme and the chief technical officer at the Benetech Initiative in Palo Alto, California.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long have you been a sociologist and a statistician?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I've been working in these tasks since my graduation from my undergraduate institution in 1988. I got my Ph.D. in 1998. I've been doing data and statistical work in human rights since 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what's the Benetech Institute?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The Benetech Initiative is a non-profit that has a series of projects which work to use technology for the benefit of humanity, including projects that develop advanced technology to detect land-mines, projects that monitor biodiversity, and projects that assist blind people to access print material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The transcript has missed the location of the Benetech Initiative. Could you give us that again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Palo Alto, California, United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's Benetech?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, it's a contraction of beneficial technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In 2001/2002 you were a deputy director of the American Association for the Advancement of Science?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The science and human rights programme of the American Association of the Advancement of Science, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And on the 3rd of January, 2002, did you prepare a report and submit it to the Office of the Prosecutor in respect to your studies on killings and migration in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I did, together with four co-authors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And those co-authors are mentioned on the cover of the report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, and their biographies to that point are included in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That, Your Honour, is P1506.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And on the 19th of February, 2002, did you prepare an addendum to that report -- did you along with your colleagues that you mentioned before --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- prepare an addendum?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And subsequently on the -- --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That addendum, Your Honours, is P1391.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And thereafter, on the 15th of November, 2002, you prepared a corrigendum to the original report along with your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, is P1394.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the reports that you prepared on killings and population movements in Kosovo in 1999, which I just mentioned, did you testify in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic on the 13th to the 14th of March, 2002, and again on the 2nd of May, 2003?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was your testimony truthful? In other words, did you answer accurately to the best of your ability and would your answers today be the same if you were asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The testimony in sequence, the three days in sequence, is Exhibit P269 -- P2690.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And finally with respect to the documents, did you and your colleagues -- or at least some of your colleagues submit another addendum to your report on the 28th of January this year?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: My former colleagues have reviewed the report, but this report was written by a different group. A long time has passed and people's interests have moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. But did you lead and supervise the group that wrote this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That last addendum, Your Honours, is P2678.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us a little bit about your past and your experience in the field of statistics, sociology, and human rights. Did you also prepare or request an updated curriculum vitae -- updated to this year?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That document had been uploaded into e-court, Your Honours, as P2791. I do not propose to go through what is a very lengthy document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But I see here, Doctor, that you have published many books and technical publications in your field of studies over the last 15 or so years. And you -- in your recent employment that we are going over, you are the director of the human rights programme in 2003 to now at the Benetech Institute?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Benetech Initiative, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see from the -- from your testimony in the Milosevic case that the crime report -- I should call it the major report of the 3rd of July was peer reviewed. It was subject to a scholarly review?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, it was the central piece of that project, and so it was subjected to two rounds of review, actually, including an extensive international team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that review -- that report, can you tell us how since then it has been received in academic circles.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. First I was, along with one of my co-authors, given an award by the American Statistical Association for the use of science, of statistical techniques in this way. That award was given to us in August of 2002 by the social statistics section of the American Statistical Association --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you go on.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I see at page 11 of your curriculum vitae a reference to fellowships and awards and I see for 2002 there is an award, a special achievement award of the Social Statistics Section of the American Statistical Association. Is that the award that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you go on speaking about how your report has been received by your peers, I see that there are two -- there are quite a few awards listed here, but subsequent to that award in 2002 you have received two other awards for your work. In 2004 the Eugene Lawler Award for Humanitarian Contributions in Computer Science Informatics of the Association for Computing Machinery. Can you tell us about that, what that was in respect of?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. The Association for Computing Machinery, the ACM, is the professional association for computer scientists in the United States. I was given that award for my design of several pieces of software, which -- the ideas of which underlie much of this work but have become mature pieces of software and released in their own right since then. It was both a technical award for the technology that we used in the -- in these -- in these pieces of software as well as a humanitarian award for the uses to which the software has been put, which is the promotion of human rights. The second award to which counsel referred is -- excuse me -- was the Pioneer Award, awarded by the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which is given annually to one or a small number of people who have promoted what in the US are called civil liberties, more broadly, human rights, through the use of electronic techniques. So those are the two awards I believe you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So -- yes. You were answering my question when I interrupted you in respect to how your original report "Killings and Refugee Flows in Kosovo, 1999," how it was received in academic circles. Can you continue that answer, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. The methods were considered very interesting in this application. As I mentioned at some length in my earlier testimony, these methods are not especially advanced in their field. They are widely used throughout mathematical demography and mathematical statistics more generally. However, the application of these techniques to human rights problems is interesting to the field. So we were asked to -- my colleague Jana Asher and I were asked to write an article for the Journal of the American Statistical Association called "Chance," which we published in the summer, the US summer of 2002. We also, as part of the process of disclosure to the court in the Milosevic case disclosed the statistical data which underlie the calculations found in all the material in the 2002 reports and most of the material in the recent 2007 report, although the 2007 report also contains new material made available to me by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just indicate to the Court that the new material which the witness just referred to has been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: So I have heard anecdotally through appearances at conferences and other speaking engagements at various universities that this material is being widely used by graduate students who study political violence. This was our intent, that we should spur a new generation of students to think about political violence in a more rigorous and statistical way, particularly social scientists but also statistical students. So our broad objective in the disclosure of this material has been, I think, to some measure achieved. Does that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. May I just follow up. The method you used in the application of standard statistical methods to human rights issues in Kosovo, how well-established or no well-established at all - can you comment on that - are these methods in the scientific community?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: There are two different methods that were used in the analysis of data in Kosovo. One of the methods was used to analyse killings, patterns of killings; the second method was used to analyse the pattern of migration. The analysis of killings used a technique called multiple systems estimation, and the purpose of multiple systems estimation is to determine, given a number of independent sources of information what might be missing from them. The reason one would do this is that the information that is missing could be in some way systematically different from the missing - excuse me - from the data which is known. This technique is very widely used and has been used for over a hundred years in the correction of censuses in the analysis of industrial processes, in the study of wildlife populations, and in many other statistical areas. To my knowledge, the use applied to human rights data has only been done in, I believe, now five countries, and my group has been involved in all of them. Principally because most human rights projects do not have the resources to do this work; it's hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And is it -- when you say "hard," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: You have to collect a lot of data and then you have to put it all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: And putting it all together means, quite literally, taking every one of many, many thousands of records and comparing it to tens of thousands of other records by hand. So, for example, in the work that we did in Kosovo, we had to make over 17.800 independent decisions about whether a particular record in one database was the same as a record in another database. However, because our results depended very sensitively on whether that decision was made properly, in no case did we allow that decision to be made only once. We made the decisions multiple times. We made every one of those match comparisons independently at least twice, and many of the comparisons were made three, four, and even five times independently by separate coders. This took several months, very intense effort, and there are few human rights groups with the statistical capacity to manage a project of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I add to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Of course, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: When we made those comparisons, of course we then compared the comparisons to each other to determine if they made the same decisions. And I'm sorry that I don't recall the precise statistic. It's in appendix 1 of the January 2002 report, but the agreement across all raters, all the people making the decisions, was in excess of 90 per cent. We had a very, very high level of agreement across the people making those decisions, and when they disagreed, we had a supervisor review all those decisions and make the final determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to focus a little bit briefly on the latest addendum, because your previous report and your previous addendum were discussed quite extensively in your testimony. Well, maybe I should start by looking at the first addendum of the 19th of February, 2002. And just briefly, you were asked by the OTP to re-run certain analysis of some of the figures and also to answer the question as to whether or not the refugee flows in Kosovo resulted from the killings, if that could be scientifically proven. And your answer basically was: No, it could not be scientifically established on the basis of the data, but that addendum did not affect any other findings that you made in your original report, in the substantive killing and refugee flows in Kosovo. Have I summarised correctly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the corrigendum of 15th of November, 2002, there you re-plotted some of your calculations and graphs as the result of three items of information that had changed, and the result of these re-plottings caused very minor and insignificant changes in your calculations, and therefore did not in any significant way affect the conclusions and analyses in the substantive report. Have I summarised that correctly as well?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, although in the November 2002 report the changes that we detected seemed to be potentially stronger than the results we had presented in the earlier report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What do you mean by "potentially stronger"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I believe that we noted in the second page that there were -- rather than there being no relationship between NATO air-strikes and killings and migration, we found that there -- that NATO air-strikes could be interpreted to have caused a reduction in killings of Kosovar Albanians. We interpreted that result as coincidental, as the result of being asked to include the entire period from early March until late May in the analysis. Earlier we had -- in our previous work we had cut off the analysis in early May. By extending the analysis through late May, we found that there was some -- what we thought unlikely statistical findings that the -- that NATO air-strikes could have negatively impacted killings simply because there were many more NATO air-strikes in May than there had been earlier. Finding many more in May would then cause this negative correlation. However, the change that we found would have tended toward strengthening the original rejection of NATO as a possible cause of the killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was -- can I ask you a question about that which puzzled me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was NATO ever a plausible cause of the killings? I can understand that NATO bombing might explain people being driven from their homes, and I can understand that KLA killings might explain that. But was NATO ever a plausible cause of people being killed? That's the type of -- the people you identify as victims here who are Albanians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't really know. We chose to explore all the alternatives that seemed plausible at the time in order to rule them out. We didn't want to exclude NATO, since that was part, at the time, of the political debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This -- your ultimate finding -- your later finding which you say is coincidental was that the NATO air-strikes could have been interpreted as causing a reduction in killings. That might make some plausible sense without trying to make a judgement of it, it may be an action that because it engages the Serbs, distracts them from killing Albanians, that I can see. I'm trying to think about the factual situation. But I can't imagine a factual situation where NATO bombing could explain a surge of killings of Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I refer Mr. Ball to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You referred to the hypothesis in respect of air attacks by NATO at page -- I think it's page 2 of the substantive report.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, that's the January 2002 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read hypothesis 2.2 and explain to the Court on what basis did you use that hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. The hypothesis was written at air attacks by the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation created local conditions that lead to Kosovars being killed and leaving their homes. The NATO influence could have either been direct because people were killed in air-strikes and others fled or indirect because local Yugoslav authorities responded to the air-strikes by killings Kosovars and forcing them from their homes. So in a sense, there's a double possibility here. Either that the air-strikes themselves were the cause of the deaths and then the survivors fled, or that local authorities were motivated by the air-strikes to either commit the killings and/or drive people from their homes. I'm not in a position to say. I'm not an expert on the specific history of the region. What we took as hypotheses were the three major armed groups that were in conflict in the region and asked ourselves: Could any -- could the actions of any of these three armed groups have caused the enormous migration and substantial killings that were observed, and that was the task we set ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you also look at footnote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- complete this? In that hypothesis, you take retaliation into account -- well, the possibility of retaliation, but you don't do that in the earlier -- the hypothesis in relation to the activity of the Kosovo Liberation Army. Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have understood that correctly. From an interpretive point of view, however, there would be no distinction between hypothesis 2.1 and 2.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You discussed in your -- can I call it the principal report. When I say the principal report, I'm referring to the report of killings of refugees in Kosovo from March to June 1999. At footnote 14 on page 12 of that principal report -- perhaps I can read the text. "The analysis considered the number of NATO air-strikes, as reported by Yugoslav government sources." And the footnote is "Yugoslav government was the primary proponent of the claim that NATO air-strikes were responsible for the killings and refugee flow in Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, where are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm at page 12 of the principal report.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Page 12, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it's footnote 14.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. At the time -- well, sometime before this report was written but during 1999, my team and I were actively following the Yugoslav government websites in order to capture information about NATO air-strikes in particular and then later KLA activity. And we found that there were many claims to that effect, that the air-strikes were responsible for the killings and refugee flow. It seemed to us at the time that this was a relevant hypothesis. In retrospect, that may seem less obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, that's -- yes, killings and refugee flow. Refugee flow, yes; killings, I still find difficulty with. The -- and you are relying on published material, a result of assertions by the Yugoslav government. Does the inaccuracy, you know, the fundamental inaccuracy of even the suggestion that NATO air-strikes could be responsible for the large number of deaths that we're concerned about, does that affect this at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe so because we disregarded those claims, as we disregarded the claims by the various deponents or -- who gave interview data about the alleged causes of their -- of the suffering they witnessed. Instead, our interest in the on-line materials that we gathered was simply in the dates and locations of the alleged air-strikes and KLA activities. Similarly, with interview material, we were concerned only with the dates and locations of the -- of the killings and the migration process. It was our intent to make our substantive inferences purely from the statistical patterns, rather than from any allegations by witnesses or by other of the primary materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to be clear about what you were saying earlier, in your corrigendum you found that there was a negative correlation between NATO bombing and population movements. But you did not draw any conclusions from that. In other words, you did not draw any conclusions that population movements or lack of population movement was the result of more NATO bombings and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the last addendum. As you indicated, you were given some additional material by the OTP and you factored those into your calculations and analyses. Can you elaborate a little bit upon the results that you got when you factored in this new material. Firstly, tell us in respect of killings what the new material was.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. The material I believe that you're referring to starts on page 6 and is subtitled "Additional Data from the ICMP, ICRC, and OMPF." These sources were provided --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: ICMP being the International Community -- ICRC being International Committee of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yes. The ICMP is the International Committee of Missing Persons, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: International Committee of Missing Persons?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: And the OMPF.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Office of Missing Persons in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Each of those three sources provided a list of deaths, of missing people identified by the date on which the person went missing and the place where the person was last known to have been seen. The people were identified by name for almost all records. We did not have time or resources to match all of these data sets to the existing four data sets. There were only three months available to us to produce this material. So we, instead, examined a descriptive analysis shown in figure 2, page 7 of this report. There are three things I think that are worth highlighting in figure 2. First I would observe that the grey-shaded area or black-shaded area apparently in the photocopy, but originally it was a grey-shaded area, shows the high and low counts summed over two-day periods for the collection of the ICMP, ICRC, and OMPF data sources. That is, we did not sum them together, since they quite likely include many of the same deaths. Instead, we simply took the high and low values from each of them for each of those periods and plotted the high and low values in a cloud that you can see is the grey area. Again, the reason we did this is that we did not have the resources to deduplicate the three data sets. We could not identify the repeated the records across them. That's, as I mentioned earlier, a time-consuming task which requires a lot of resources. The scale of the ICMP, ICRC, and OMPF data is shown in the left vertical axis. That is the top value, the maximum value reached in any two-day period by the three sources is 439 deaths. The grey area is overlaid by a black line, which is the original estimate we presented in the 2002 report. It's labelled at its peak as the MSE estimate. Its scale is shown on the right vertical axis. It has a maximum of 1.226 deaths in a single two-day period, which happens to be the first point of the graph. The core conclusion that I take from this graph reaches back to the analysis that we drew in the 2002 report, which is that the pattern of deaths and the pattern of migrations, but deaths specifically in this graph, follow a three-phase rising and falling structure, rising in late March to an early-April -- late-March/early-April peak, and then falling again -- falling - excuse me - for the first time toward 0 on the night of the 6th/7th April; remaining at a low period between the 7th of April to the 10th of April, when they begin to rise again to a mid-April peak. After the mid-April peak, the number of killings and migration that is shown in another graph decline to a low period in late April. They rise again to a series of peaks in late -- at the very end of April and early May. After early May -- after the 11th of May, they continue at a very low level until the conflict ends. The principal conclusion from this graph is that the new data are nearly identical to the old data. They are extremely similar in pattern, and there is no reason to believe that adding these data would change the results. In fact, it's quite likely that adding these data would increase the precision of the results substantially, since they show such a very close relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So how many data sources now have you -- are you now able to rely on in respect to these patterns that you mapped in this graph?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: This graph includes seven independent data sources, including the interviews from Human Rights Watch, which are the smallest of the seven, going on to the interviews conducted by the American Bar Association, Central East European Law Initiative, and their Kosovar partners, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, and the exhumations conducted by the first-round of exhumation teams provided to me by the OTP in 2001. To those four sources, we've added these three, the ICMP, ICRC, and OMPF. This graph may be easily re-drawn, and I would be happy to provide it to the Court, if it were interesting, showing all seven lines. It is a bit of a mess, seeing seven lines on a single graph, but to my eye, they show precisely the same thing with seven independent lines. So I found this presentation much clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may actually be of interest to see the seven independent lines. Can we take it that it's not possible to combine all seven into one graph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's not possible to -- I mean it -- I'm sorry. Let me ask -- let me clarify to make sure I understand the question. I can put seven lines on one graph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. But what we're looking at here is two separate figures, one based on four sources and one based on three.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you do one based on all seven or is that not something that would assist us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could certainly do so, but to do that would require that I deduplicate the three sources that I've just received, the ICMP, ICRC, and OMPF. In order to include those three sources with the others, we would have to determine which of the deaths in each of the three new sources are in common with each other and in common with the four existing sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a weakness of the three new sources that you haven't been able to distinguish the deaths that may be replicated among them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's less a weakness in the data sources than a weakness in the resources available to us to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's a deficiency when compared with the work that you've done on the four original data sources.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was thinking about that this morning as I woke up horribly jet lagged in my hotel room. There's nine hours' difference from California. And what I realised is that the first graph in appendix 2 of the substantive report addresses specifically that point. And so if I could ask you to turn to page 36 in the January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think what we'll do, if you don't mind is -- we've overrun already to the point where I think we're probably exhausting the others who are serving us. So what we'll do is have our break at this stage and return to this point after the break. The usher will show you where you should wait while this break occurs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if you could please leave the courtroom with the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 20 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When we broke you were speaking about a weakness or a deficiency in the amount of time you could work with the last set of data sources that you got in respect to the last addendum, and you were about to explain the nature of this by reference to page 36 of the principal report.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. As I mentioned earlier, the purpose of the estimation of the total deaths was to consider whether the deaths we did not know about would be in some way systematically different than the deaths we did know about. So in figure 2 that we observed before, figure 2 of the most recent report, the one submitted in January 2007, we saw this dark black line marked "Multiple Systems Estimates." It's the one that I believe is still on the screen. I'm not sure what screen I'm looking at, but it says "Courtbook Sources." And if you compare that graph to figure 1 on page 36, it's figure 1 of appendix 2, page 36 of the January 2002 report, again we see this very consistent pattern of the three-phase structure where the -- there is a bulk of killings in the early period, late-March/early April, that fall dramatically to a period between the 6th and 7th of April until about the 10th, and then there's a rise again around the 10th to a peak approximately the 15th to the 18th, and then it drops down in late April and so forth. What figure 1 shows is the deduplicated total for the four systems we talked about earlier, that is, this is not an estimate. These are the counts, the simple number of deaths reported to Human Rights Watch, the OSCE in the exhumation data and in the American Bar Association and their partners' testimonies. In some sense, this addresses the Court's questions to me about the impact -- yes, that is the correct graph that's now on the screen. Thank you. This addresses the Court's question to me about what the change introduced by the estimation might be, and the answer is very little. There is very little change introduced by the estimation process. In fact, the -- while we were greatly concerned about potential statistical biases inside the four systems, once we had done the estimates, we found relatively little bias, as evidenced by this comparison. There's a variety of other tests that we can discuss if there's interest. I think that most germane for this discussion is the striking similarity between the line in figure 1 that's on the screen now and the lines that are encapsulated by the grey area describing the ICMP, ICRC, OMPF patterns. Again, what that means is that the new data, the data that's just become available to my team now, is substantively identical to the data that was available to us in 2001 when we did this work. I feel, therefore, very confident that if we were to be given somehow additional resources to do this to include these three sources into the four we have now, the results would not change, except that the errors would decrease. Our precision would improve, which is the way of all -- of all science. If you have additional resources, you can repeat the experiment, you can get more data. If you got it right the first time, your results won't change but your errors will decrease.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you touched on, but could you briefly in layman's terms, briefly, just explain the reasons for the difference in the count for the two axes in figure 2 of the 2007 addendum. The vertical axes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. I believe this is now on the right side of the screen, is this the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. The axis on the left is showing the total numbers represented in the grey area, that is the high and low values of the ICMP, ICRC, and OMPF series. So, for example, on approximately the 28th of March or perhaps the 1st of April - I'm not sure of the exact date - there were 439 deaths reported in one of those three sources. That's the peak shown in that grey area. Another of the sources showed considerably fewer, but there's a range in there, and I think that it's important to observe the range, because this is -- that's natural with data -- with data that's collected ad hoc, as these were. It was not a probability sample. The axis on the right that has its maximum at 1.226 deaths shows the range in the black line labelled MSE estimate at the mid-April peak. This line is the same line as that presented in the earlier work, in the 2002 work, and is the estimated total number of deaths by two-day period throughout the period 24 March to 11 May. Again, we did the estimate to control for bias. Reference to figure 1, which we've just covered, suggests that that concern may have been excessive, but statisticians are very sensitive to the possibility of bias. So we -- but we expend a lot of energy worrying about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on quickly to figure 3 of the latest addendum. That is dealing with the refugee flows, and briefly, if you could explain what does figure 3 indicate in respect to the use of the new data from the UNHCR in respect to refugee flows.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. There are three series shown here -- or four series - excuse me - four -- three series in solid lines, though they have slightly different weights, and one series in a dashed line. The three series in solid lines are the three series that were used in our original reporting which first appeared in a report from AAAS, from my employer at the time the American Association for the Advancement of Science entitled "Policy or Panic" in which we analysed -- we presented the first analysis of migration. The fourth line, the dashed line, comes from what purported to be daily refugee counts compiled by the United Nations High Commission for Refugees in Geneva, and these were provided to me by the Office of the Prosecutor several months ago. Now, there's a couple things that I think are worth observing here. First, in many of the particulars, the series are very similar. In -- there are some differences, but what's -- the crucial pieces of agreement for the argument are the decline on 6/7 April, which is of substantial importance, the relative low period between the 7th of April and the 10th of April, the peak in mid-April, the decline in late April, and then the series of small peaks later, in late April and early May. That phase structure is intact in all three structure series. However, I'm skeptical about the quality of the data from the UNHCR Geneva because it has a few anomalies that suggests to me that perhaps the data they have received may have been averaged over a series of days.
