They may have received a block count for a week and then they projected it backward by dividing the number by 4 or something. Seems, for example, when we look at the flat line between about the 5th of April and the 10th of April, well, that's implausible to me that exactly the same number of refugees would cross every day. That's not really how refugee movement works. Refugee movements ebb and flow, even a little bit, but to have an identical number across a series of days is very unlikely. And so what's much more likely is that someone at some point said, well, we've just gotten a new report, we know it covers this period, so in order to create daily counts, we'll just divide by 5 or something and present those as daily counts. When we compare in particular the UNHCR's reports from Geneva to those reported both in Kukes, which was very near the flow, or in Tirana where their press office was where I got the data, it's clear that the data from Albania was much more detailed and up-to-date or more current as time passed. It may be that later in the process, the two series came together a bit more as UNHCR improved their communication process between Albania and Geneva, but in the early period I'm pretty skeptical about the Geneva data. On the whole, I do not believe the new data has any substantive impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remind me what EMG is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Albanian government formed an Emergency Management Group which was charged with trying to handle the influx of so many hundreds of thousands of people into Albania. In addition to the refugees crossing directly into Albania, Albania was also receiving a lot of refugees being transferred from Macedonia. So the EMG was charged with this charge. They did not begin work immediately. Their work really began in ernest in mid-April/early -- mid-April. And at that time they began releasing daily or even semi-daily reports of the number of refugees crossing. When they did that there was a period of about a week or ten days. We can refer to my published data, it's shown there, in which both the EMG and the UNHCR continued to publish daily reports, but at some point, they got together and said that's enough and UNHCR stopped publishing those reports and then the EMG took over and did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I use both series because they cover -- although they overlap, they cover different parts of the period. They both drew on same sources, however, which were the OSCE border observers who were hand-counting and the Albanian border guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you do not believe the new data from UNHCR has any substantive impact. Impact on what? Could I ask in respect to your major findings, in respect to population flows and the three surges followed by troughs, do they have any impact on that finding at all?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: One might argue, although I think it would be on weak grounds, one might argue that the trough between the 6th of April and the 10th of April is not as low as it is in the UNHCR data as it is in the other data. Now it's not clear to me that that would make a significant substantive change in our argument and furthermore, as I argued earlier, I think that's based on an artefact of the way the data was interpreted in Geneva. One would be very hard-pressed to explain how refugee flow could appear from the point of view of Geneva to have been identical for five days in a row; that seems very unlikely to me. However, that would be the only difference it makes. From all the other points in our argument, the patterns are substantively identical. There is, for example, a difference in very early April where the series close to the ground, in particular, the Albanian guards at the border and the UNHCR in Kukes and Tirana show a slight decline, whereas on the same two-day period, the UNHCR shows a peak. Well, UNHCR Geneva shows dips both before and after that. Again, that looks to me like they aggregated the data from before and after and then post hoc reported it as a single day. I think one would be hard-pressed to put more credibility in data that was collected or was reported from farther away from the conflict when it shows so many anomalies as the Geneva data does, relative to the data that was captured at the border or very near to it, as was the case with the Albanian guards' data, the UNHCR Kukes data and the EMG government, not Albanian government data.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move to figure 1, figure 1 which is on page 5. I'd like you to explain figure 1 in the context of the statement that you make at page 4. I'll read it to show you where I want you to direct your explanation. "Both the 2002 and 2007 analyses used conservative coding rules in order to give the KLA and NATO hypotheses the fairest possible test, that is, if there were any possibility that the KLA or NATO could have caused migration or killings, the municipality was quoted as inconclusive or coinciding. The coding scheme that produced the categorisation in the table above 1, that is table 1, which I will get to later, may have yielded excessively conservative results for these reasons." In that context, can you just briefly in layman's terms explain figure 1?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. Our objective is to consider in more depth the argumentative device that was discussed at some length in my earlier testimony before the ICTY, in which we discussed how we might interpret a statistical pattern as a cause or not a cause of another pattern. And one of the fundamental points that we argued at the time was that in order to be a cause that the purported causal act had to precede the purported result. So if NATO bombing, for example, would cause migration, it had to precede it. If NATO bombing followed migration, it could not said to have caused the earlier migration. However, the question is: How long would it be between the NATO bombing and the migration before that purported cause would have dissipated? And for the purposes of the earlier discussion, we said it would either have to coincide saying it occurred in the same two-day period or it would have occurred in the previous two-day period; that is to say, 0 to 4 days in the past. If a bombing occurred 0 to 4 days in the past, it was considered to have coincided with a peak in migration or killing. If, however, the air-strike occurred more than four days in the past, that is to say more than four days before a peak in migration or killing, it was coded as inconclusive, which is that it could have possibly been a cause but that we were skeptical. We would ask: Why didn't people leave sooner? What we find, looking at figure 1, is that we divide the peaks in killing and migration between those that occur before the 14th of April or after the 14th of April. And we then say of the peaks in killing and migration that occur before 14th of April -- the 14th of April, which is most of them, by the way, we find that nearly 60 per cent of them occur with no prior NATO or KLA activity. A very small percentage on the order of 10 per cent are inconclusive, which is to say there was KLA or NATO activity but four or five days prior. And there's a intermediate fraction on the order of 30 or 35 per cent which coincide, which is to say that KLA and NATO activity occur within four days prior to the peak in killing or migration. After the 14th of April, we see a somewhat different picture. There's a much greater proportion of inconclusive events, and this we separate out to highlight, that as the conflict wears on, inconclusive events, according to this definition, will necessarily accumulate simply because there's more time in the past available for a NATO or KLA activity to have occurred. This does not make that NATO or KLA activity a more likely cause; it's simply that there's more time. If the conflict's been going on for three days, it's impossible to have an inconclusive event because our window is four days long. If the conflict is 20 days old, then there are 20 minus 4, 16 days, in which an inconclusive event may have occurred. By the time the conflict is 60 days old, we now have a 60 minus 4, 56 possible days, in which a conflict may have occurred -- an inconclusive - excuse me - event may have occurred. So as time goes on, we believe that this notion of inconclusiveness becomes spurious and what we would like to do is raise to the Court's attention the weakness of this kind of analysis. It is for this purpose that statisticians use the kind of analysis we used in our original report, which is multiple regression, because it takes these sorts of relationships into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The result of this excessive conservativism which would result in excessive inconclusive findings we see represented here in table 1, can you comment on table 1. In a general sense and in layman's terms, does the factors noted in table 1 coincide -- does not coincide inconclusively. What do they indicate in terms of the cause that might have affected the killing and population movement during the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you understand what I'm asking?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. As one examines the cells of table 1, there are three values in each of the cells, three possible values. So considering the upper left-most cell for the municipality of Decani, we find that the relationship between the KLA and killing of Kosovar Albanians is inconclusive. What this means is that the peak of killings in Decani is preceded by one or more interactions between the KLA and the Yugoslav authorities; however, those activities occur five or more days prior to the peak of killings. That's what inconclusive means in this context. If we move left -- rightward - excuse me - in the cell, the word "coincides" indicates that the peak of killings in Decani, killings of Kosovar Albanians, coincides with a NATO air-strike that occurs 0 to 4 days prior to the peak of killings. If we move to the end of that row, we see that if we look at the peak number of migration, people migrating out of Decani, we find that there is no prior NATO air-strike. There is no NATO attack that precedes that peak. So those are the three possible values available in the cells of this table. As we observe in our analysis, peaks are not the only time that people move. There are in some cases smaller peaks or plateaus, and so we do not recommend to the Court that this kind of analysis of simple peaks be overinterpreted; rather, the broad patterns of rising and falling should be the focus because peaks can be surrounded by other similar peaks or they can be isolated alone in a field of 0s. For examples of that, I recommend that people review the 29 graphs which follow at the end of this report, where we show municipality by municipality killings, migrations, KLA activity, and bombing, and we see a bewildering array of possible combinations. The combinations are, indeed, bewildering even to me, and I've been looking at these data for more than six years. That's why statisticians reduce them to more direct analyses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If would you look at this table, table 1 overall, is this consistent with or inconsistent with a pattern of killings or migration being caused by KLA activity or NATO activity -- NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I believe that for many municipalities it is inconsistent; for other municipalities it is inconclusive. I do not consider it an adequate test of the hypotheses. We have done it because in prior questioning it was a source of considerable discussion, and so for purposes of complete transparency we have presented it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say it is inconclusive, can you explain that a little bit further. I understand when you say it is inconsistent with the hypotheses that the refugee movements and killings could have been caused by NATO bombing or KLA activity, but when you say it is inconclusive --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- just elaborate a little bit on that. Is it something that -- or would the table indicate that the movements are not related or are unlikely to be related?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I think this is -- the notion -- let's see. How can I explain this? Finding that patterns coincide with each other is a seductive -- is a seductive finding. What is necessary in statistical argument is not simply that patterns coincide when they both occur, but rather, that they also coincide when neither occur. This analysis only allows us to examine the former. So, for example, as a metaphor, we could say that it is true that on every 24-hour period that an air-strike occurred in Kosovo during this period, the sun rose. We would find a perfect coincidence between the sun's rising and an air-strike occurring. However, there were many days on which the sun rose and there was no air-strike. Therefore, it's clear that the sun does not cause the air-strike; rather, they are irrelevant and spuriously related. It is unfortunate that analysis such as that presented in table 1 is unable to distinguish between the spurious coincidences, such as that I describe in the rising sun metaphor, and real patterns such as those that would be found in the regression analysis presented in the original report in 2002. As an example, we can consider Pec. Pec in table 1 on page 3 suggests that for all four of the relationships of interest, there is a coinciding relationship between NATO's potential impact on killing -- excuse me - KLA's on killing, NATO on killing, KLA on migration, and NATO on migration. If we refer -- I'm sorry to whoever is creating the images. I'd like to turn to page 18. At the top there's a graph of all four patterns in Pec. If we expand now just to go to the top. Thank you. That's perfect. We can see that there is a sequence of KLA activity throughout the period, some of which is followed by migration or killing, some of which is not. Similarly with killings, some KLA activity is followed by killings; in other cases the killings precede the KLA activity, such as the peak at the end. Bombings follow a similar pattern. In this case table 1 would, in my opinion, mislead us to thinking that there was a relationship between killing and migration and the KLA and NATO activity, whereas a more detailed examination shows that, rather, Pec was simply a very active -- a very active site of both NATO bombing and KLA activity and, perhaps coincidentally or perhaps not, migration and killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the conclusion from that, I take it, is that the use and analysis of the new additional information does not in any significant way affect the patterns that you found in your principal report of 2002?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And to a great extent, the data used confirm the accuracy -- the new data confirm the accuracy of the data used and estimations made in respect to the principal report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The new data, if you are referring to the data used for killings that we discussed -- I'm sorry. I've lost the page. It's probably page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: ICRC, ICMP, OMPF.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Correct. If you are referring to those data, yes, they, I believe, confirm the validity of our earlier analysis. Validity, precision, and accuracy are terms of art in statistics and so -- that have slightly different meanings. So for us, we would say they confirm the validity of the earlier analysis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dr. Ball.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but there's something I have been trying to work out here which I can't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a little while ago you said, when you were referring to that table 1, that for many municipalities it was inconsistent and for others it was inconclusive. I do not consider it an adequate test of the hypothesis. We have done it because in prior questioning it was a source of considerable discussion. Now, what is it that you've done --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- that you don't consider to be an adequate test and please try to give me a brief answer to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. So I think that if we can refer to the graph on Pec, it provides an excellent example. If we can go back to that on page 18, because Pec is an especially complicated place. Okay. You'll notice that both of the lines on the table have a series of different peaks so that for migration we see a very -- a strong, early peak which turns out to be the dominant one and then two later peaks, one immediately before the 7th of April and one late in May, both smaller peaks. The analysis in table 1 is focussed only on that first peak. It treats all the other peaks as though they're meaningless, as though they're irrelevant, and it does so because of the nature of this analysis where we're examining the coincidence of the peak as though there's only one, but, in fact, there are three. In other graphs, if we were to examine other municipalities, the relationship between peaks is even more complex, and we could go into those in detail if it were of interest to the Court. But I think we can examine the line for killings in Pec and find an equally complex story, where we have a series of small peaks in early April, a larger peak in mid-April, and then the largest peak, actually, at the very end of April. The problem with the analysis in table 1 is that it can only take into consideration the dominant peak, the single highest peak, rather than taking into consideration the series of peaks which, in my opinion, better represent the pattern in any given location, in any given specific place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it that's in table 1 that causes us difficulty? I'm sorry. I'm lost on this completely at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I do not understand this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's in table 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not understanding what it is about table 1 that confines it to one peak and why, indeed, you did this at all. I just don't understand what's going on here. I'm sorry about this, but I'm completely baffled by this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, my apologies for that. I -- this was actually originally requested of me in the -- in my prior testimony here, and so we have presented it for completeness since there was no additional opportunity to present it in the previous case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you're saying is you're presenting something misleading for completeness and I'm having difficulty with this concept why one would do that in the first instance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I guess only because I was asked. I don't really agree with it and I would prefer to look at a more complex measure, such as that presented in the second appendix of my first report; I believe that is the measure which takes into consideration all of this variation and all of the necessary complexity to understand the relationship among these four patterns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The same report, the page immediately before the table.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in the largest paragraph there which starts "In the first analysis ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see in there that this is in fact confined to one peak only, and that's the bit I was missing I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That I assumed that this was simply a repetition of the same type of analysis as before, but this is confined to only one peak for each municipality. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the same as that presented in the original report in figures -- let me give you the precise cites. The original report showed these as figures 8 and 9 in the 2002 January report. And we presented these after we had shown the original patterns and just prior to the figures that we believe are conclusive, figures 10 and 11. And this is in the 2002 -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the report, your latest report --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- you deal with how you proceeded before at the foot of page 1 and into page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is that an example or is that a process different from the one set out in the paragraph we're looking at further down the page so that it would identify various peaks? Or is that again a description of the same exercise confined to one peak carried out in 2002?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The latter, Your Honour. It is confined to one peak. We were asked specifically to explore figures 8 and 9, which are confined to one peak. We have a very brief comment on this weakness in -- on pages 5 and 6, but it is very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When I read this report, I -- where does it say that this is unsatisfactory? I've read this thinking this is a genuine update of your conclusions, but I'm now getting from you that this is an exercise that you're not happy with. Now, where do I see in this report that you're unhappy about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that if we read the section on page 5, which I'm looking for now. I will point it to you directly. When we stress over and over again the excessively conservative nature of this report, that is what we are saying. We are saying that we believe that this overstates -- that this analysis overstates any potential relationship between NATO and KLA activity and potential killing and migration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. And I really hadn't got from this the message that this was unsatisfactory, but thankfully it's been clarified in the oral evidence. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The primary task of this report was to incorporate the -- or compare the additional data that you were presented with to the earlier data you used and I understand from what you are saying is that the results of that analysis does not in any way change the analyses and conclusions in your principal report of 2002?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Without going over that report in detail -- but turn to it and just refresh briefly. The report at figure 2, I think, if you could just briefly elaborate on that in layman's terms briefly, because remembering that you have done so to some degree before. It indicates that there are three distinct surges or patterns in the killings and refugee flows, and these distinct patterns in the killing flow also coincides with the distinct patterns in the refugee flows.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is -- is indicated in figure 2. Do you have that before you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in figure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In case you're in doubt, I have no difficulty following that. It's the simple -- the simple part I think are -- if anything here's simple, that part I had grasped.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that part I take it is the pith and gravaman of your findings in respect to the patterns?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, this is the basis for our conclusion in the first hypothesis that there is likely a common cause of both killing and migration, which was the basis for the subsequent analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And at figures 10 and 11 you used those graphs to demonstrate the conclusions that the killings and refugee flows were unrelated to NATO bombings or KLA activity.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: More precisely, what we tried to show in figures 10 and 11 is that if we control for the effect of what is known about KLA actions, KLA interactions with Yugoslav authorities and NATO air-strikes, the underlying pattern of killings in figure 10 and refugee flow in figure 11, those underlying patterns remain substantially the same. That is, if we used the statistical relationships between KLA activity and NATO activity and killings in figure 10, we are unable to explain the pattern. We can only remove a small amount of its shape. The remainder of the shape, the residual, in statistician's talk, shows the pattern after the KLA and NATO activity have been controlled. Since the patterns are the same, our interpretation would remain the same and we would discard the hypotheses that either the NATO or KLA, together or in combination in this case, can explain the pattern and consequently could be plausible causes of the killings. Figure 11 is very similar, although the pattern is slightly less clear. We also in the appendices present these analyses by region, for the east, west, south, and north. Or maybe not. I'm sorry. Let me look for them. Mm-hmm. No, they're presented only as tables, not as graphs. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your report at page 15 --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, figures 20 and 21 show them by -- show the killings and residuals by time and region. Yes. Pages 58 and 59 -- or -- sorry. 59 and 60, figures 20 and 21. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The report at page 15 --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your report at page 15 --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- section 5.4, you speak of a circumstantial link between Yugoslav Army activities and the observed pattern of killings and refugee flow. The extreme decline in the number of killings and refugee flow observed in the period of 6 and 7 April coincides with the unilateral cease-fire by the Yugoslav authorities in recognition of Orthodox Easter. Can you elaborate upon that very briefly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I want to know is the extent to which, in statistical terms, is there an indication of a causal link.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: There is no indication of a causal link. Let me be quite clear that observational statistics do not permit an affirmation of cause. Observational statistics are at their limit disconfirming hypotheses or rejecting hypotheses. As we have done here, rejecting the hypotheses of NATO or KLA causality with respect to killing or migration. However, we observe coincidences, and coincidences may be evocative and helpful for other determinations of fact. In the case alluded to here, in section 5.4, we note that on the evening of the 6th of April the Yugoslav government declared a unilateral cease-fire in recognition of Orthodox Easter. This cease-fire was not respected by NATO or the KLA. They increased their operations, doubling and tripling them, according to the databases published by the Yugoslav government in particular, although with -- supplemented by other sources as we discussed in our appendices. What is interesting to us and what I've mentioned several times earlier this morning is that during the period of the cease-fire, from the early morning hours of the 7th of April until Saturday, the 10th, killing and migration in most regions declines to its lowest point throughout the conflict to that point. It declines in many places to 0, in other places to near 0. So the Yugoslav government declares a cease-fire, killing and migration go down towards 0, NATO and KLA activity go up, doubling and tripling, but no activity -- no more killing and migration. On Saturday, the Yugoslav government announces that because NATO and the KLA are ignoring the cease-fire, they will resume operations. They resume operations and we observe that killing and migration begin to increase again. Not immediately to a peak. The peak occurs a few days later sometime between the 13th and the 18th depending on which of the series we observe, but it does begin increasing on Saturday the 10th. This is a coincidence. This is not proof that the Yugoslav government was the agent of killing and migration, but it is, I believe, an important statistical coincidence which could be useful in the balance of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. There is nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order will be: General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic, Mr. Sainovic, General Lazarevic, General Lukic, and Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Before I start, Your Honour, a number of my colleagues are going to cross-examine Dr. Ball, and we'd like to ask about the rules on cross-examination here. I'm not sure that the rules apply in any event to an expert, but if they do, we'd ask Your Honour for some leeway for a number of reasons. First, Dr. Ball, in the original 65 ter estimate, was going to be a six-hour witness. Secondly, there had been additions to his report. And thirdly, unless we've misinterpreted the Trial Chamber's ruling respecting Dr. Ball's testimony, we seem to get some indication from that that the Court might provide additional time for us on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We think the indications that have been given of the likely lengths of cross-examination are reasonable in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I just indicate, just briefly, that I -- Dr. Ball traveled a long distance to get here and got here not in the best of health. So I would ask the Court to grant him whatever dispensations he might need in terms of time maybe just to step out for a while. He could indicate if he needs to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will do that, will you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Ball. I'm Norman Sepenuk and I'm an attorney for General Ojdanic. Before I get to your statistical analysis, I would like to spend a small amount of time on background and context questions so we can better understand your testimony, and I want to start with your report, your 3 January 2002 report, Prosecution Exhibit 1506, which is killing and refugee flow in Kosovo March/June 1999, 3 January 2002, and this report was presented to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I notice that on the front of the report there are two particular organisations which are mentioned, the American Association for the Advancement of Science and the American Bar Association Central and East European Initiative. And can I ask you why these two particular organisations appear on the front cover?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Because they were the sponsoring organisations for the production of the report. At the time, I worked at the American Association for the Advancement of Science. My co-author Wendy Betts worked at the American Bar Association/CEELI. A number of the other authors were associated as consultants with those two organisations and we had our organisational homes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. And you note on the second page of the report, though, that these organisations -- that the opinions expressed in the report are not the opinions of the organisations but rather you and your fellow authors. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in your acknowledgement to the report, you state: "US government support was essential to the project and support was provided among others by the United States Department of State and the US Agency for International Development." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That support was provided to ABA/CEELI, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your acknowledgement you also state that the report would not be possible without the collaboration of a number of organisations and individuals. I won't name them all.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But I notice among them are the Human Rights Watch, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, and the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in your acknowledgements you also mention that your earlier report which you referred to in your direct testimony published in 2000 called "Policy or Panic, the Flight of Ethnic Albanians" that -- and you mention also a number of individuals and organisations who contributed to that project and one of them is a Mr. Fred Abrahams who worked for Human Rights Watch. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, as I understand it, it was Mr. Abrahams and a gentleman named Eric Stover who originally invited you to go to Albania in mid-April 1999 to undertake the project?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: They invited me considerably earlier and independently of each other, but, yes, I ended up there in early April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in "Policy and Panic" in your acknowledgements in "Policy and Panic" you state, "Fred Abrahams from Human Rights Watch and Eric Stover of the Human Rights Centre of the University of California Berkeley originally invited me go to Albania in mid-April 1999. Subsequently, they introduced me to the project's co-director Fron Nazi, East-West Management Institute for the Policy on Legal Studies. Fred, Eric and Fron oriented me to the region, told me what I needed to read --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please, if the speakers could slow down while reading. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'll slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: "-- provided many feedbacks, helpful feedbacks on many drafts and gave me access to their interviews for confirmatory qualitative evidence." Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that at least in these early stages of your research, Mr. Abrahams, for example, was sort of a mentor to you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, Dr. Scheuren was a mentor to me. I'm a statistician. Fred's a human rights analyst. Fred and Fron and Eric showed me information, provided data, told me stuff about Albania that I could use, but mentor is too strong a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. But at least you respected Mr. Abrahams's factual knowledge of the area and his views on various subjects?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So as I understand it, you went to Kosovo in mid-April 1999 to gather data for a potential report.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I went to Albania originally to figure out if there was a report that could be done. We found one, but at the time it was pretty up in the air. We weren't sure what we would find.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. And how long did you stay in Albania in the early stages?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: In the first visit about two weeks, about two weeks or a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you went back when?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I went back to the US in early May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then back to Albania?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: About two and a half weeks later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And then what? Just give us very briefly again the evolution?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I began recruiting a team of Albanians and Kosovar Albanians who would act as a survey group. My original intent was to build a team of people who would survey refugee camp residents on a probability sampling basis, that is, we would sample probablistically households from tents and then interview them about their experiences before and after their migration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And if I can just interrupt you briefly.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm trying to get some timing here. At least you were still doing your research, let's say, in July of 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, we were long done by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You were long done by then?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Because when we realised that NATO was going to intervene, we had to radically restructure what it was we were doing. We weren't going to be interviewing people in camps, because the camps were going to be empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But I take it by that time, let's just say July 1999, you hadn't yet reached any conclusions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I had actually -- at that point I was not at all sure what the project was going to look like. I didn't--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly request for both speakers to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers make pause between question and answer for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... is it fair to say --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. May I -- I was interrupted by the interpreters. May I complete my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We had, really, very little idea even what data we had collected, because things were very hurried in the last weeks of June, mid and last weeks of June, and so we had no interpretation whatsoever of that material in early July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. And the only thing I'm trying to get at is, at least by that period, let's say July of 1999, you hadn't yet reached any conclusions based on your statistical analyses?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But is it also fair to say that aside from not reaching any conclusions based on your statistical analysis, you had already reached the conclusion at this early stage that the Serbian defence establishment had a plan to expel ethnic Albanians from Kosovo; hadn't you already reached that conclusion, Dr. Ball?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That was a working hypothesis, but by no means a conclusion. Conclusions are reached by data and not by anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And what was your working hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: My working hypothesis was that there had been some kind of process that had driven people from their homes. What would that be? Clearly, one of them was that there had been a process of ethnic cleansing. Others were that NATO bombing or KLA activity had caused the migration and the killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Wasn't that a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, you really both need to -- MR. SEPENUK I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- allow time, because Mr. -- Dr. Ball is answering you very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need some sort of gap between the question and answer to enable the interpretation to catch up. That's why you had that problem a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll be very much aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: When you said a working hypothesis, what I'm asking you is: Hadn't you already concluded that there was a plan by Serbian forces to expel ethnic Albanians from Kosovo before you ever even started to do your statistical study?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to read your question on the screen here, and you -- if I understand correctly, you've asked: Had I already concluded such a thing. And I can tell you: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's look at a transcript of a radio programme that you had.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: In July 9th, 1999.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It was radio talk, "Talk of the Nations Science." Remember?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Iris Flatow --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- was the moderator. And you appeared on that program?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I did, and we talked about Operation Horseshoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm trying to get at, sir. You haven't mentioned that yet. And let me go on, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in that programme after you had said that you hadn't yet concluded the results of your statistical analysis, you said: "What's interesting is that the Yugoslav defence establishment made public a plan for ethnic cleansing. Well, it wasn't a plan about ethnic cleansing. It was a plan, a strategic plan, to attack the KLA, the Kosovo Liberation Army, back in October/November of last year, the defence establishment was very clear that this was what they were going to do. It was called Operation Horseshoe." Now, tell us -- first of all, you said it was made public. Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is not an objection, but since we're referring to a document, could I just have the reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Certainly. 3D518 - excuse me - 3D518, page 377 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are we ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm waiting for it to come up on the screen. Is there a problem with finding it? Here we go. You're right at the right spot now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you see what I just quoted from?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So tell us at that time in July of 1999 what you knew about Operation Horseshoe and how you happened to know it.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, there was a lot of talk about it among all the journalists who were in Albania at the time, and I certainly heard their talk. This influenced my formulation of hypotheses. I thought if these people are right, what we should see would be a horseshoe. If you look at my subsequent published material, you'll find that's not at all what we found. That's a hypothesis which was rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you say this was -- your understanding is this was made public by the Yugoslav authorities? That's what you say in the radio programme.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I believe the German Defence Minister, if I recall correctly, make remarks about this for which he was later in some trouble, but it was public.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did you later find out that that report was completely fake? Did you find it out either yourself or from Mr. Abrahams who wrote about it in Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I heard that it was fake, yes, but as you'll note, we didn't use it. I mean, I think that this confirms the scientific process. Even when you find something that's fake, when you go to the data and you don't find it, you discard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on here what you said in the radio programme. You said: "Our hypothesis is that if ethnic cleansing matches, the pattern of refugee flow matches that plan, that will be very interesting evidence that, in fact, the refugee flow is a product of that plan. We can't say precisely why. We'll then go back to witness and refugee testimony. We'd go back to forensic evidence to make those links more tightly, but this is, as I said, the sort of topographic map, as it were, of this process," correct. So you already had -- before you even had any results of this statistical analyses, you had a so-called topographic map based on what you now say is an erroneous notion about Operation Horseshoe which started, even if it did exist, even if a plan did exist, against the KLA and then transferred to a plan to expel all ethnic Albanians. That was your notion at the time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, sir, that's not correct. In fact, you're taking a series of subjunctive statements and making them indicative. What I said is that one could imagine that we could have a hypothesis and, if these patterns were to match, then things would be interesting. What I'm stating here are a series of hypotheses to be investigated. I stated those hypotheses before we had evidence to investigate them -- well, we had the evidence, but it wasn't analysed. And when we finally did analyse it, as is clear from the published record, we discarded those hypotheses because they were inaccurate. I believe this is the process of all science, that all science begins with hypotheses, Most of which end up being discarded in the face of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, when you wrote --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please make pause between question and answer? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... previously talked about, didn't you already have in mind then or hadn't you already concluded then that there was this pre-existing plan by Serb forces to expel ethnic Albanians?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. At the time you wrote "Policy or Panic," which is the year 2000, didn't you --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- hadn't -- pause for your answer, sir. My colleagues are continually reminding me of it, and I apologise for not doing that, to you, to the interpreters, and to the Court, and I'll try from now on out not to mess up anymore. And my question is: At the time you wrote "Policy or Panic" in the year 2000, isn't it fair to say that you had already concluded, aside from any statistical analysis, that there was a pre-existing plan by Serb forces to expel ethnic Albanians from Kosovo? Yes or no, sir, if you can.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: When I published "Policy Or Panic" in 2000, I had found that we could reject the hypothesis that NATO bombing was a plausible cause of the migration. We at that time had very limited data on -- well, I had no data on the KLA, and I had very, very limited data on killings, so our sketchy conclusions about other topics were, again, inaccurate, but our finding about the -- excuse me -- about bombing and migration has been sustained throughout our later work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- I'm sorry. Let me just read to you specifically what you said in "Policy and Panic."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And this is 3D516 at page 232, and maybe you want to wait until it comes up so you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: 3D516, page 232. And if you just -- no, the second paragraph, please right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You say, if you could follow long: "The findings in this report suggest that the Yugoslav military, police, and paramilitary apparatus may have used the bombing as a broad political excuse to conduct a previously prepared operation to evict ethnic Albanians." That's what you said, correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And that previously prepared operation, was that the erroneous and non-existent horseshoe plan that you have previously testified about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, let's observe two things about this sentence. First, we use the term "may." We do not use the term "prove" or "did" and I think that's important. So I'll pause that the interpreters can translate the subjunctive. Second, I think it's essential to note that we do not link -- or in this case, I, because I was the sole author of this particular work, I did not link the claim about a previously prepared operation to any specific operation, such as that you've just referred to. So, no, by this time the whole operation horseshoe thing had been clearly discarded, and what we're suggesting here is essentially the same kind of language which appears later in my reports when I observe that there's a coincidence on the night of the 6th and 7th of April that when Yugoslav forces cease operations, migrations and killings also cease. That, too, may suggest that Yugoslav forces are responsible. However, let me draw your attention to the lack of the word "proof" here. As statisticians working with observational data, we do not make such claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We'll get to that later.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as you say -- you say that Mr. Abrahams originally invited you in April of 1999, Mr. Abrahams and two others, to go to Kosovo and undertake this project and one of the things that these folks told you, they told you what to read. Do you remember that? That was -- say yes. You have to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did Mr. Abrahams suggest that you read his article of August 15th, 1958 [sic] in the International Herald Tribune in which he stated that the first priority of the United States policy should be the indictment of Milosevic. Did he direct you to that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I suspect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. I can remember, Mr. Abrahams, and I doubt if he was physically capable of writing that article in 1958.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did I say that, Your Honour? No, no, August 5th, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not specifically remember what he asked me to read, but I think it probably was more Human Rights Watch reports than media reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did you read that media report or did you discuss his personal views about Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Certainly I discussed his personal views of Mr. Milosevic as I have with dozens of other people, probably hundreds of other people, including, in fact, Mr. Milosevic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you of course shared Mr. Abrahams's views about Mr. Milosevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I really didn't know. I never worked on the Balkans and my expertise was Central America and South Africa, so I really was more interested in getting into the story than sharing anyone's views. Fred and I were colleagues but didn't know each other that well when we started working together in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: When you say you really didn't know, you had certainly well prior to your testimony in the Milosevic case, you had formed some certain opinions about Mr. Milosevic, had you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, but you're eliding three and a half extremely turbulent years of research. In 1999, when I first went to Albania, I didn't really know what I was getting into.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But I'm talking now about 2001 --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: When I'm writing --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: July 14th, 2001, when you were at that hacktivism conference?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your remember that, sir? In Las Vegas, Nevada?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And it was presided over by Reid Fleming from The Cult of the Dead Cow?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I sure do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And The Cult of the Dead Cow being what?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: They are a self-proclaimed hacktivist group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And were you on their board of advisors?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm on the board of advisors of their hacktivist group, not of The Cult of the Dead Cow itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I may have missed it and if I did, I apologise to you. Is that in your updated curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, I haven't done any work with them for years. Would you like to know what they do, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Right now they are trying to produce, and they have been for some years, produce software that would enable dissidents in China to make their views known throughout the world without repression by the Chinese authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And at that conference you said as follows: "Of course now on the basis of crimes of war we have tribunals. Tribunals which try people who have violated international humanitarian law and send them to prison. It would be very nice if we had a round of applause for the extradition of Slobodan Milosevic to The Hague last week." And then the record indicates applause. "And I hope you're all excited as I am by the prospect of his very pleasant and drawn-out trial which will begin in about six months." You said that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I did indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And were you also excited about the prospect of going to The Hague some months later to testify at his trial?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I had no idea at that time that I would be invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You had no idea. Okay. And you said later on in that conference, and I quote directly, you're talking about human rights, and you said: "Let's work with those rights and then push them. If you want more, let's keep pushing, absolutely, keep going, no reason to stop now, we've got some momentum. We've got one of the worst bad guys ever in jail, at least in my lifetime." You said that, correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you were referring to Mr. Milosevic, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I do not recall. It could have been Pinochet but it's in the same period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Is that serious testimony?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Are you serious about this? You really don't think it was Milosevic. I mean, the whole talk was in the context of Kosovo and Mr. Milosevic. You're not saying that you weren't referring to Mr. Milosevic there, were you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly who I was referring to. The talk was not all about Milosevic. The talk was actually all about technology and I had several sections of it about Guatemala and there were also several sections, if you recall, about domestic US situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind me if you would when Pinochet was in jail if at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- he wasn't really in jail. I don't remember. But this is an activist conference so I would have been making fairly off-the-cuff remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Off-the-cuff remarks but truthful remarks do you think?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Truthful remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm willing for the record to say that I was referring to Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, that's all I wanted to know. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a suitable time for us to interrupt, Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Lunchtime, Dr. Ball. The usher will show you where you can wait -- well, where you should go. We'll resume in about an hour at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Chowhan will be absent on other authorised Tribunal business this afternoon, and we have decided that it's in the interests of justice to continue with the sitting in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this afternoon, every time the interpreter interrupts to remind anyone about the failure to observe the pause, we will deduct five minutes from the time for cross-examination. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I wasn't going to mention it but I will mention it now. I'll mention another fault of mine and that is when I switch from this mike to the mike in the middle, I thought it was on the same channel, 4. It wasn't. It was on a different channel, so I actually never heard the interruptions of the interpreter. Now, I didn't hear it because I had it on the wrong channel. That's no excuse, particularly, but that's the reason and hopefully that won't happen again. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, when we broke, you were frank enough to state for the record that it was indeed Mr. Milosevic you were referring to at the hacktivism conference when you said we've got one of the worst bad guys ever in jail at least in my lifetime. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I take it, though, that you didn't feel or don't feel that your personal feelings about Mr. Milosevic in any way prevented you from being objective in your testimony at his trial?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: What I testified to then and now have to do with the statistics, not with my opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And actually the main reason -- or at least one of the reasons I'm asking you that was -- it's based on an article that appeared in the report Wired News of July 16th, 2004, and the article's entitled "Hacktivism and How it Got Here." It's Exhibit 3D519 at page 387. And if you can put that up, I'd appreciate it, so you can read along with me. Yes. And it's beginning: "Ball spoke." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: "Ball spoke about hacktivism at a hacker conference in the summer of 2001 and during his talk made a disparaging comment about Slobodan Milosevic, former president of Serbia and of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Ball later testified against Milosevic at the war crimes trial in The Hague. When Milosevic cross-examined Ball, one of the first questions he asked him was, Who was This Dead Cow Cult?" And you said: "My under oath spin to Slobo," Slobo, I take it meaning Mr. Milosevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: "My under oath spin to Slobo was that hacktivism is an opportunity for engaged, young programmers to do cool and socially beneficial stuff with their technical skill and curiosity instead of getting in trouble, said Ball, and I actually believe that." My question to you, Dr. Ball, is what did you mean by "your under oath spin"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: People -- the question that underlay that was: How could you say that the Cult of the Dead Cow was about cool and socially beneficial stuff. And I said: I wasn't talking about the Cult of the Dead Cow, I'm not part of the Cult of the Dead Cow. I'm not part of the hacktivismo group which you and I clarified earlier. And I said: What I meant to Slobo, which I used in the slang term spin, was that hacktivism is a way to try to keep what I think is the most the brightest and most engaged generation of my time out of trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: My question is actually a little bit broader than that. Maybe I didn't make it clear. I take it you agree with me when you're under oath you don't spin?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But you did say "my under oath spin." So at least at that point apparently you did spin a bit; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No. What I did is explain something in a slang term to a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, I want to discuss with you some of the difficulties of understanding a massive phenomenon that you've been testifying about such as the ethnic Albanian refugee flow from Kosovo during the period March to May of 1999. Now, I assume you would agree with me that purely qualitative methods such as refugee interviews have their limits. I think that can be answered yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the first limit, the obvious one, is that there are far more people involved than can realistically be interviewed, yes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's a resource question; that's not a yes or no question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Then answer it however you want.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Okay. If you had sufficient resources and you had a small enough context, you could interview everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. But in this case probably unrealistic, correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Probably unrealistic in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then second, there's the inherent problem of whether the interviewees, the people interviewed, are telling the truth or telling their story accurately and, as a corollary, whether the interviewers are getting the information down correct. True?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's actually pretty tricky. That's a tricky question because there are many inaccuracies which can enter an interviewing process which turn out to be irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: So, for example, if you were taking a deposition of a witness about a particular event, but the witness provided you with extensive details about some other event and she were to get many of the details about this other event wrong, that would actually not affect the validity or the usefulness of the interview for your purposes since the event you're interested in she got right. So it's actually pretty complicated. The validity of an interview depends not on the interview itself but rather the purposes to which you intend to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: My question might have been a little simple-minded. All I meant what that interviewers and interviewees are human beings and sometimes they make mistakes? That's all.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Sometimes they make mistakes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And third, and perhaps most importantly, is that these interviewees -- there was no random sampling of the interviewees; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, that's unfortunately not correct. Some of the interviews were conducted by random samples; others were not. Physicians for Human Rights, which was the basis of much of our migration analysis, was conducted by random sample. The first two components of the IPLS survey that we conducted in camps, which we discussed earlier, particularly in late May and early June, were conducted by random sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Wouldn't you agree that a substantial number, though, of the interviews, were not conducted by random sample? For example, Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, Human Rights Watch was the smallest of the sets. I'm afraid I don't know what you mean by a substantial number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, let me be more specific. You advised Mr. Abrahams at Human Rights Watch on the statistical analysis violation chapter in their book, correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And there's a chapter in that book and it's Prosecution Exhibit 438, e-court page 444, which talks about limitations of the data and it says as follows -- if we can put it up, Prosecution 438, page 444. There it is. And at the top, if you'll bear with me, in the first paragraph there it says -- again, you were an advisor on this chapter. It says: "Most importantly, Human Rights Watch did not randomly sample the interviewees. On the contrary, researchers purposely sought out not only the victims and witnesses of violations but specifically those with knowledge of the most serious violations such as torture, sexual violence, and executions. Therefore, these data cannot be extrapolated to general findings for Kosovo as a whole." You don't disagree with that statement, do you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I represent to you that Sandra Mitchell of OSCE also testified here to the same effect. I just mentioned that to you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That would be logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, you considered three -- because -- because there -- these interview techniques have these shortcomings, you undertook -- that -- one of the reasons is that you undertook your statistical analysis, correct, in view of these shortcomings of the purely interviewing techniques, one reason that you proceeded was that reason, shortcomings in interviewing techniques; therefore, you wanted to come up with a more authoritative study based on statistical analysis.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I don't think "authoritative" is the appropriate word.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What would it be?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We wanted to use a method which would be able to account for the spaces or under-reporting which necessarily occur in the sorts of surveys or interview processes that the four samples we had available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Fine. And you considered three possible causes --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- of the refugee flow?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you're quick to point out in your report, that's Prosecution Exhibit 1506, I'll read it, I don't think there's any dispute about it, so I don't think we have to put it up on the board. You said in the report: "It is beyond the capacity of statistical analysis to prove that any of these hypotheses is the definitive cause of the patterns seen in the two forms of violence." Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to the first cause here, and that is the NATO air-strikes. Now, I understand you restricted yourself to just two sources, at least when you first started to undertake that research, there were going to be two sources, one, Yugoslav and press reports and press reports from Yugoslavia, correct, which is ultimately what you used. And you were also going to US Department of Defence information; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That was an original idea, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you, as I understand it, on the department -- there were two things you were going to do. One, the Serb sources and, two, the department of defence. As I understand it from your testimony in the Milosevic trial, you didn't proceed with the Department of Defence data or trying to get that data because as you put it: "My two phone calls to the US Department of Defence went unanswered."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That was the extent of your trying to get information about NATO bombings, two phone calls?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. As a human rights activist, I do not have extensive contacts at the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, who did you call there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The public relations office I got from the internet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: From the internet. And you never got a live person? What did you do; leave a message?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No. I spoke to someone who said they would get back to me, and they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then what did you do? You followed up on it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And that was the end of it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You didn't make any effort to go there to talk to anybody?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You didn't write a letter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You didn't send a fax or an e-mail?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Don't you think it would have been at least interesting to have that information other than the information from Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, it's interesting you should ask that, because several years later I ended up at a conference with a couple of guys from I think it was the Air Force War College on bomb damage assessment in Kosovo, and when I told them this, they laughed at me. They said, of course they didn't call you back, they were never going to give you that data. We would never release information like that, not even years after the event. So I think that while it may be an interesting point to debate here now seven years after the fact, I think that my initial assessment has been borne out by discussions with people who told me that I was never going to get that data, no matter how hard I tried for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- and that concerns the diligence of your efforts, but we won't argue. Now, after the NATO bombing, you -- as I understand it you next considered the hypothesis whether actions by the Kosovo Liberation Army motivated Kosovar Albanians to leave their homes; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the information on KLA activity, again as I understand it from your report, was obtained from interview accounts and a variety of non-governmental reports summarised and provided to the project by the ICTY; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Some of them came from that. There were also web site reports, again from the Yugoslav government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, you attached an appendix, appendix 3, "Additional Sources of KLA and NATO Activity"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Let's first look at the -- at the interviews, and what interviews are you referring to here? You said "interview accounts."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, the interview accounts would have been those given to the ICTY, principally, since the ICTY was conducting investigations and they provided me with a database of those materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did you -- and so the interviews are primarily, if not exclusively, of Albanians. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I don't know. As I said, they came from the ICTY, so at that point I was unaware of what the original sources were. All I knew is that they had come from the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did your interview -- did your research and the general knowledge you gained about the area ever indicate to you that ethnic Albanians generally are hesitant, to say the least, to implicate the KLA in activities for fear of reprisals?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's outside of my competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you never learned that, for example, ethnic Albanians who collaborated with Serbs or even did business with Serbs were being abducted and killed on a regular basis? You never learned that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, I can't say that I've heard of a systematic report about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Forget about systematic report. Did you hear about it at all?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I've heard plenty of rumours about lots of violence in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But you didn't try to do anything to track down what you thought to be rumours and confirm it was really fact?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I relied on the sources that are listed in appendix 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And how about Serb civilians, were they interviewed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
