utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to refer to my earlier answer. I've answered that already. The interviews came to me through the ICTY database, principally. The other materials here are documentary sources that are available that you can refer to if you're of continuing interest. The interview materials, however, were provided to me by ICTY, and I do not know what or who the original interviewees were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, you say they also came from a variety of non-governmental reports, for example. Could you give us some examples of that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: There were reports by the European community monitor -- they're listed here in appendix 3. I'm not sure which -- if you want me just to read it or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, no, no, not at all. I have them and I -- but you said non-governmental, whereas in this appendix, there are various governmental sources, for example, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Ministry of Defence, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Were they consulted?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Their websites were consulted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And What did you find on their websites?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I found listings of moments of conflict between Yugoslav authorities and KLA authorities in Kosovo during the period of study, and we coded those as attacks, killings, and bomb attacks, where there was no exchange of gun-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did you remember or did you -- did you remember seeing a so-called White Book published by the federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs in March 2002 containing some 958 pages -- and that's defendant exhibit 3D182 -- which gave detailed accounts of KLA attacks, KLA terrorist groups attacking civilian, army, and police both before and during the war, do you remember that 985-page book?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, did not look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did not look at it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Don't you think that would have been a helpful source of information?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: It may well have been. On the other hand, it may well have simply reprinted the material that's available in the rather copious other Yugoslav government sources that are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You don't know that. You're speculating?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm speculating. Do you think that they came up with a great deal of additional evidence in that period?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Believe me, sir, if I could testify in this case, we would spend the rest of the day here? Let me just ask you questions.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did you consult the publication issued by the VJ, the army General Staff, in June 2001, defendant exhibit 3D133, setting forth again 206 pages of KLA terrorist attacks on the army, MUP, and civilians, both before and during the war? Do you remember that at all, sir?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand it, you didn't -- you also didn't consider in your analysis, data on whether NATO and the KLA were working together in various combat operations, did you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We did not consider qualitative evidence of that kind. We considered some kinds of quantitative evidence of that kind, but as I reported, I believe I testified in the 2002 appearance, the statistical data does not support the claim that there was an interaction between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Nor did you consider, as I understand it --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, you're mischaracterising what I just said. What I just said is that I did consider it, okay, let's be clear. I did consider it, but there was no statistical basis for continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. I accept that. Thank you. Nor, as I understand it, did you consider that there may have been advanced warnings to the KLA of NATO bombings so that civilians could flee the area. Was that a potential possibility that you thought about or considered?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm puzzled by your question. Can you restate it without starting with "nor" since that's the point we just clarified four lines above.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did you consider whether -- whether there were advanced warnings by NATO to the KLA to -- of bombing so civilians could be evacuated from the area?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: As is clear from my report, we considered only violent clashes between KLA and Yugoslav authorities. We did not consider any kind of verbal warnings by anyone to anyone else about any activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's all I'm asking. Did you consider data that indicated that ethnic Albanians sometimes left their villages on orders or instructions of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I believe that's a restatement of the previous question and the answer is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the answer is --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get to the third hypothesis and that is that refugee flows and killings resulted from actions by Yugoslav forces. All right. You state in your report that the statistical analysis and correlations cannot prove that the Yugoslav forces were the external influence responsible for the observed patterns. However, the findings of this study are consistent with the hypothesis that action by Yugoslav forces was the cause of the killings and refugee flow. Did I state that accurately?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's roughly accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, similarly, and perhaps more clearly in the Milosevic case, it's 3D521 at page 19967 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: By the way, Your Honours, the Prosecution has now added the 2003 Milosevic testimony to their exhibit, but they only did that yesterday. So prior to that, we had made a separate exhibit out of it not knowing that the Prosecution was going to add it. So this is contained in both the Prosecution exhibit and the Defence exhibit that I just mentioned, 3D521. It's transcript 19967.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you said as follows: "We include no data on Yugoslav forces or force movements. It is for that reason that there is no statistical analysis in this report of Yugoslav activity." Do you remember that? Testifying to that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And in your most recent report, that's the report of January 28th, 2007, revisiting killings and migration in Kosovo, you said: "These three hypothesised causes are KLA activity, NATO air-strikes, or a systematic campaign conducted by Yugoslav forces. Because of available data, we're only able to consider directly the first two." Okay. And finally on this point, so there's no mistake about it, I'd like to quote from your article, Statistics and Slobodan, written by you, I believe, with Jane Asher in 2002. This is after you testified on the Milosevic case. Statistics and Slobodan is the name of the article, using data and analysis and statistics in the war crimes trial of former President Milosevic. And by the way, this is one of the publications included in your updated curriculum vitae. And in this report you said: "There was no data available to us that detailed Yugoslav government force deployments or movements during the period in question. We could not, therefore, directly test the hypothesis that Yugoslav forces were responsible for ethnic Albanian deaths and migration." Do you remember that, writing that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you -- I may have missed it in all your prior reports, Policy and Panic and this report, and so forgive me if I have, but could you tell us why you could find no data that detailed Yugoslav government -- the deployment of Yugoslav forces. Why couldn't you find any data? I -- please enlighten us on this.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We found some data, but it was too skimpy, too scarce, too patchy, to be considered sufficient. We found, for example, that there were huge bases in some places and there were some supposedly armoured groups in other places. But those were far too -- at too gross a level to provide us with information. They were not individual attacks, the way the KLA data was detailed. They were not specific air-strikes, the way the NATO attacks were detailed. So we were unable to do this calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I guess -- I'm sorry. I guess what I don't understand is you were able to find the KLA data without apparent difficulty --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, let's say with difficulty. I don't want to minimise what you did. You were able to find the KLA data. Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And why -- you said you were able to find some data on Yugoslav force deployment, but it was too skimpy. Where did you look? Who did you talk to? How did you go about doing this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I talked to some military analysts that I had met in Washington and they didn't know much. They said that the Department of Defence probably had it and that would have been one of the things I would have asked if I had gotten through to anybody at public affairs --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You mean if you had completed that phone call? Go ahead. Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: But they were very skeptical that I would find anything. And the KLA and NATO data was actually not that hard to find, counselor, because it was on the Yugoslav government websites.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: How about the 958-page report put out by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs well before your reports were written. Couldn't you have consulted that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: One of the things that I think is interesting to consider when we're looking for statistical evidence -- there may be a parallel idea about this in law. You'll have to tell me. I don't really claim to understand the law --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I hope you don't think I understand statistics.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Don't worry, counselor. Is that evidence that goes against interest is much more weighty than evidence that goes in favour of interest. So the evidence that was presented in realtime by the ministries -- the Yugoslav ministries on their websites was far more interesting to me and continues to be far more interesting to me than anything that would have been published by them subsequently, because anything that was published subsequently, would have had the opportunity to be sanitized, whereas things that were published in realtime, had a very clear focus. It was written on the website. The websites were titled with names like The Denouncement of Criminal NATO Air-strikes and so forth. So the intent of those websites was quite clear. I felt confident with that material because it was evidence against interest. By using the evidence published by the Yugoslav authorities, that struck me as the strongest possible case of the test of NATO or KLA involvement. Using Yugoslav government information on their own troop movements post hoc would have, and to this day, would strike me as highly suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: How about KLA troop movements, what did you use for that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: KLA troop movements are not part of the analysis. What's part of the analysis, sir, is interactions between the KLA and the Yugoslav authorities. Bombings, injuries, casualties of Yugoslav authorities, those are all denounced rather loudly in the websites that were published contemporaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that the reason you didn't get any information on Yugoslav force deployments was that you were unable to do that because you couldn't find any action of Yugoslav forces independent of interactions with the KLA. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, in fact, that strikes me as absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, then let me refer to your article "Statistics and Slobodan."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: 3D520, page 394, 3D520, page 394, if you'd kindly put that up, please. And could you blow it up on the left side there. Yes, there it is. What you just said was absurd, Dr. Ball --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: -- mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- is exactly word for word what you said in this article. "We were unable, however, to obtain data on Yugoslav Army activity independent of interactions with the KLA." Can you reconsider your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, because that statement is out of the context of this discussion. "We were unable, however, to obtain data on Yugoslav Army activity independent of interactions with the KLA from the sources" - and I'm sorry we didn't include this in the article - from the sources that were used for this analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact, sir, that the actions by forces of the KLA and Yugoslav forces was so closely related in both time and place that it's virtually impossible to separate them. Isn't that a fact, Dr. Ball?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, that's not a fact at all, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And given the dynamic that we've been talking about, isn't it fair to conclude that the most that can be said is that ethnic Albanians fled the area where combat was occurring between the army or between Serb forces and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You've just assumed that my rebuttal to you was an affirmation. Perhaps you should review. What I said is that, no, that's not a fact at all, to my knowledge, and then you restated it as if I'd affirmed it. Should we go over that again? I don't think we've understood each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then, give me --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Give me your statement.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: My statement is that I have -- I do not believe that it's the case that actions of forces by the KLA and Yugoslav forces are so closely in time and place, it's impossible to separate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you accept it as one reasonable alternative, though?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I think we would need a lot more information about Yugoslav force activity before such a thing could be said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Which you never looked into?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I looked into and wasn't able to find, but let's consider a thought experiment, Counselor. One way to think about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way a statistician would consider this problem is to think about the relative sizes of the two forces. If the two forces were in some way similar in size, then the proposition just made might be reasonable. However, all the evidence suggests that the two sizes, the size of the Yugoslav forces and the size of the KLA were radically different --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you there for a moment. Have you ever heard of a gentleman named Bislim Zyrapi, who was the commander of the KLA, who testified in this courtroom that the KLA numbered about 18.000 people --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- and had turned from a guerilla army into a regular --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- army or more or less regular army with a guerilla capacity and supported by a good percentage of the Albanian population. Would that change the dynamic, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, my analysis looks at the amount of interactions between the KLA and the Yugoslav forces. Notwithstanding any testimony that has been given here, looking at that data indicates that there was relatively little going on between the Yugoslav forces and the KLA. Consequently, it seems to me highly unlikely that there was either parity in size or an extensiveness in interaction through this period. Consequently, I disagree with the statement which you put into my mouth -- well, it's scrolled off the screen now -- in which you said that -- well, we'll have to scroll back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, what I'm respectfully suggesting to you, Dr. Ball, is that like you, those fleeing refugees were also -- just like you couldn't distinguish activity independent of interactions with the KLA and Yugoslav forces, that refugees were also not able to distinguish actions of Serb forces and the KLA and they were simply fleeing the combat area where there was actions between two opposing forces, and I'm saying, don't you at least accept that as a reasonable possibility?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, no, I don't, because part of the point of this entire analysis, sir, is to show that over time and space, the interactions between the KLA and Yugoslav forces do not coincide with the flows of refugee movement or of killings. If your supposition were to be correct, we would see interactions between the KLA and the Yugoslav authorities at --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Which you never got any data on; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps we should review. In appendix 3 we have two pages of the lists of them, and I have subsequently published online the database of the KLA and Yugoslav force interactions. Have you reviewed those? Those might answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Continue, please. I'm not here to answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No. I'm just trying to clarify. I'm sorry. But the -- in that on-line material that's been online since my 2003 appearance and here in appendix 3 we detail our sources of KLA data, that KLA data is on interactions between the KLA and the Yugoslav forces, precisely the kind of conflict which -- hello? I'm sorry. There's been a --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I think it's okay. I think you can go on.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Okay. Precisely the kind of conflict which, if I understood your question correctly, you imply people would confuse and therefore flee. Well, whether or not that's true, those conflicts came after most of the killing and migration had been completed. That's the point of the 29 graphs in the recent report, that's the point of the regression analysis in the January 2002 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And my point was only that the actions of the Yugoslav forces - in your article it says Yugoslav Army, but I think you meant Yugoslav forces - activity independent of interactions with the KLA, you could not find, and our contention is they were inextricably interwoven but, again, this is not the place to argue. It is up to the Trial Chamber for later consideration. Let me just turn to my last point here, and that is what you call -- you say that you can't directly test the hypothesis that Yugoslav forces were responsible for the migration and killings of ethnic Albanians, but you do say that there's one important circumstantial factor and that is the -- what you call the -- it's on section 5.4 of your report, Prosecution Exhibit 1506, and that is -- you say: "One of the findings of the study shows a circumstantial link between Yugoslav Army activities and the observed pattern and killings and refugee flow," and then you cite "the extreme decline in the number of killings and refugee flows observed during the period 6/7 April, 1999, coincides with the unilateral cease-fire declared by Yugoslav authorities in recognition of Orthodox Easter." Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Ball, may I suggest to you that an alternative reason for the drastic decline in refugee flow is that immediately after the announced cease-fire at 3.00 a.m. on 7 April 1999, the Yugoslav authorities shut Morina border point and the daily number of refugees entering Albania fell from tens of thousands to under 2.000 until the border re-opened on the morning of 10 April 1999. I suggest to you that that's another -- at least another alternative reason why the refugee flow declined to almost 0. Isn't that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: It is a fair statement, and we considered it at length.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Would you like to understand the reasoning why we do not consider it an important --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Sure.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: -- factor?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, for two reasons: First, because killings match the pattern precisely and it's not my impression that closing the border at Morina would have stopped the killing pattern -- so the killing -- the decline was not only in migration; it was also in killings. So that's the first of the two reasons why we did not consider that especially significant. The second is that our analysis is of people crossing the border. Our analysis is of people leaving home, and in the "Policy or Panic" report, we -- or at that time I explain in rather tedious statistical detail how we projected backward, people leaving -- from people crossing the border into people leaving their homes. So we are not measuring people crossing the border, which would be immediately vulnerable to precisely the argument you raise but, rather, people leaving their homes, which is the measurement of much greater interest. We do not, upon looking at the transit times that people experience in mid-April, find a dramatic change. It's not as though we found that people had been held up all of a sudden for three or four additional days in mid-April compared to earlier April. Rather, people simply weren't leaving their home during that period, so it's not as though it hasn't been looked at. It's been looked at and discarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, people, of course, were leaving their homes and there were long lines of refugees. Do you not know this, that there were long lines of refugees, when the border was closed --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: -- mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- long lines of refugees were turned back by --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- Serb authorities and told to go home.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's right. Those were people who had left their home before the 6th of April. What we're interested in here is people leaving their homes between the 6th of April and the 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I don't think you know that, do you? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: What's the "that"? I'm sorry. You've lost me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You say these are people who left their home before 6th April?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, if they were turned back on the night of the 7th of April, it seems a fair guess that they left their homes on the 6th or before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you remember being interviewed or -- by the "Guardian," the "London Guardian" on March 21st, 2002? This is 3D522.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I don't remember this specific interview, but you'll no doubt put it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's pointed out to me that there's no answer on page 103, line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, there is an answer. Or is that the -- is that your question in both lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe we can clarify it now. I'm not sure we should go back, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I don't understand about this, Mr. Ball, and perhaps you can very simply explain it. I understood perhaps wrongly that you gathered your statistical information from people who actually crossed the border.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if the border's closed, what's the source of information from which you can work back to the point where people leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a great question and we spent months trying to think that through. What we had done is conduct several thousand interviews among people who were in refugee camps principally in Albania but also in Bosnia and in Macedonia. And among the questions that we asked them in several different surveys, some conducted by my teams and others conducted by Physicians were Human Rights or Human Rights Watch, were when did you leave your home in Albania and when did you cross the border? Okay. So those are two different dates. Now, very often those were the same dates; other times they were different dates. When they were different dates -- when they were the same dates, we calculated the transit time, the time people were on the road between their homes and the border. We used that pattern to create a model of how long it took people to cross the border and that model varied by when people were leaving their homes and when they were crossing the border. So we were able to change the model as necessary to reflect the differing conditions that people faced through the course of the conflict. This is all detailed in the appendix to the Policy or Panic report. And the point -- the precise point of this goes to the question at issue here, which is, what happens when the border closes? Do people stop leaving their homes or do they simply queue up in a long line? My understanding is that, for the most part, there were a lot fewer people leaving their home; perhaps, not 0, there may have been some, but there was still a lot more people leaving their homes both before April 6th and after April 10th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I -- it's no doubt me again, but I don't understand what the source of that information is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand how a model can assist you in a situation where the point at which the information is being gathered is closed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we weren't gathering the information from people who were specifically at the border. We were gathering the information retrospectively in late April and May from people who were in refugee camps in Albania and Macedonia. And we were asking people in late April/May, When did you leave your home in Kosovo? And they might say, On the 2nd of April. And then we'd say, Well, when did you cross the border leaving Kosovo into Macedonia, Albania, or Bosnia? And they would say, The same day or a day later or two days later or we went to stay with our cousin and then came six days later or what have you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did that exercise not throw up a block of answers that demonstrated that no one was crossing the border when it was closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we found and that's documented in some detail in the Policy or Panic report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, just to finish up here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That 3D522 on page 489. Down at the bottom there, when you were explaining what happened after the cease-fire and you said, "Coincidentally enough, the number of refugees and the number of people being killed falls to zero, bang. Right to zero like the door was closed." And I simply suggest to you, Dr. Ball, that at least another reasonable explanation for the decline in refugee flow was just that, the border was closed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Presumably that was a question, so could the witness be allowed to answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp wants to swap chairs with me, obviously. That answer -- or, sorry, that quotation from you, which is that the number of refugees falls to zero, can you explain what that means, bearing in mind the two different points that are relevant, that's the point of crossing the border and the time of leaving home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. This was a very -- I remember this interview vaguely. It was a very long interview and I don't think that this is the complete context of what I told the journalist. The number of people crossing the border and the number of people being killed does fall to zero or towards zero. Falling to zero is a term of art. It doesn't mean that things go completely to zero but it does go pretty close to zero. Could the door be closed, is that an explanation? It's a possible explanation, but it fails to account for the number of killings following that pattern almost identically. It also fails to account for our transition -- excuse me, our transformation of the data from people crossing the border to people leaving their homes, via the model I explained earlier. This model, transforming border-crossing time into home-leaving time, was a major focus of the Policy or Panic report and I'd be happy to elaborate on it if it would please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk, in the cross-examination by Mr. Milosevic, there were points made about the point of crossing the border and whether it was, in fact, the Morina crossing point that the information was being gathered at. Is that no longer a matter of controversy?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I think it could be, Your Honour, but in the interests of this -- a lot that's going to be covered today. Quite frankly, I have only the vaguest notion of what my colleagues are going to cover but that could very well be covered in subsequent cross-examinations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Ball. How are you doing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm well. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're holding up all right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You can make it another hour?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because I fly here from Texas and that's seven hours so I know what you're feeling like I think. When you started your testimony today you told the Prosecutor that you were a sociologist and a statistician and the first question I have is in relation to your educational background. According to your CV, you got your bachelor's of degree in 1988 from Columbia University in New York in sociology?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then in 1991 you got a master's degree in sociology?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in 1998, you got a doctorate of philosophy degree in sociology?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And wrote a thesis, Liberal Hypocrisy and Totalitarian Sincerity, the Social and Idealogical Origins of the National Human Rights Movement in El Salvador, Pakistan, and Ethiopia, which just from its title seems to me to have nothing to do with statistics, but pure sociology?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Sociology at the University of Michigan always nearly always has a substantial quantitative component and I think if you refer to chapter 5 you'll find plenty of statistics there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that dissertation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't have any degrees in statistics though, do you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume you've taken a course or two though?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: A course or two. Nine semesters, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I was being a little bit facetious when I said a course or two. In the analysis that you did in this case, I take it you attempted to be logical in that process?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And logic is important to the analytic kind of thinking that you do, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it you studied some logic in college?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you studied the important logical principles?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in your analysis in this case you attempted to apply some of those logical principles that you studied in college?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of the principles you applied was the principle of the undistributed middle?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: In what context do you refer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In context of your analysis of the data in this case.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm not sure how you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, tell the Chamber what your understanding is of the principle of the undistributed middle?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I don't know the principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You do not know the principle?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that it was first -- that it was first annunciated as long ago as Plato in his dialogue?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Never read those?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I read some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me give you a syllogism that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my microphone over there keeps coming on and I don't understand why. I've turned it off three times now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask that the other microphone is also switched on because we don't hear the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think your voice is not perhaps being picked up as clearly as it had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They've told me they need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're familiar with a syllogism like this, I'm sure. All the goats have long hair, Jim has long hair, therefore Jim is a goat?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that illustrates the fallacy of what is called the undistributed middle, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That illustrates a fallacy, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, there's also a scientific discipline, is there not, which analyses data using fuzzy logic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you're familiar, I suppose, with the proposition that fuzzy logic was first suggested, I guess, I say suggested, and -- in a paper by a scientist by the name of Zadik?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to object to this line of question. I think it's really a matter for the Court to control but it's going too far now. The cross-examination should be focussed on the reports of the witness and not generally as to syllogisms or ancient principles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, one can always question an expert about the techniques and systems that he used to arrive at the conclusions that came from his analysis. And right now I'm exploring those with him to see how many of those he paid attention to, how many of them he used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think you can trust us not to require the entertaining prompting that you've been good enough to favour us with so far, but we'll be able to get to the crux of it fairly quickly and it would help, I think, if you did, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll get there quickly, Your Honour. I promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to know if you applied fuzzy logic in your analyses in this case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what the best-selling statistics book of all time is?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I don't know, but I suspect I can guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you guess Darrel Huff's book?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Probably, either Darrel Huff's or "Misused Statistics" by Spirer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Darrel Huff's book has sold over half a million copies. It's entitled, "How to Lie With Statistics"; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you're familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I've glanced at it a few times. I know what it contains.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know that one of the things he writes about in that book are misleading graphs; don't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you recall this, that he says with regard to misleading graphs, that they can result from unintentional bias on the part of the researcher.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I don't remember that particular quote, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, according to him, if he's correct, that even if you don't intend to allow bias to creep into your research, that a misleading graph can result.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That would be a truism, yes, sir. I mean a truism in the sense that it's unfalsifiable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The old --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we can use an example and I don't -- let's look at P2678 on page 7, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Which report do you refer to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's your most recent one. This is a graph we've already looked at today, so you'll recognise it immediately when it comes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if we can just enlarge that middle so we get a good shot of that graph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, we've already discussed this at length, but what you're doing here is you are taking new material from ICMP, ICRC, and OMPF, and superimposing it over a graph that contains earlier material that you were using at the time of your early testimony in Milosevic. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the way it's displayed here, it appears, if you just glance at this graph without knowing -- without getting some kind of a serious explanation about it, if you just glance at this graph, it looks like the data in many ways matches up fairly closely with the earlier data, if you look at where the peaks are and the height and stuff like that, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Indeed it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's because this graph was constructed not as a stand-alone graph but as an overlay, even though it doesn't say that it's an overlay, that's what it is, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know what you mean by an overlay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me tell you what I mean. You use one scale for the old data where the high point in it is 1226 [realtime transcript read in error "526"] and you use another scale for the new data where the high point is 439, but when you overlay them, the high points wind up at the same place, therefore making them look like they track each other?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm afraid we have some slippage on what we mean by track.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: If I can explain, the point of this graph is not to show that the scales are the same, but to show that the peaks and valleys are the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: May I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Any correlation analysis will disregard differences in scale. This is an analysis of the correlation between the two series. Therefore, the difference in scale is not relevant. In fact, scaling them to be the same enables us to see the correlation. That's the point of the graph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I wouldn't know that if you didn't explain it to me. If I was just glancing at it, I would be struck by the similarities, especially in the height of that first peak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just been pointed out to me that page 113, line 19, where it says 526, what I really said there I think was 1226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to have the usher show you a really crude little graph that I've drawn and I emphasise crude. This isn't a beautifully computer-constructed or anything like that. What I've tried to do is use 1226 as the high point and put that new data kind of where it belongs. We can probably put this on the ELMO and then we can all see it. Now, what I've done is used your 1226 scale to put in the 439 data, basically, that you see kind of in red down there and that's very inartfully drawn, but in terms of raw numbers, that gives you a more accurate view of what the raw numbers look like between the two sources, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, what's our objective? If the objective is to see the total -- the absolute values, that's correct. If our objective is to ask the question: Would adding new data to the old data change the results? Then I'm afraid that your graph tells us relatively little. What we might ask if we wanted to use both graphs is what would be the correlation coefficient between the two series. It's not reported here, but I can calculate it for you rather trivially and I remember anecdotally that it's on the order of 0.75 which is extremely high. So the graphs are not different and I don't dispute that your graph is also informative, however I do dispute that it is the appropriate graph to use given the question we're asking in this particular context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, one of the things that I know you are concerned about is data integrity and this shows a rather wide variance of data from different sources, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, not at all. The point is that we have count data, which is simply the data that's available to be counted in the three new sources as opposed to estimate data which takes into account the data which was not countable. Therefore, they are not series which should be directly compared; they are series which should be compared in terms of their peaks and valleys which is done in figure 2. They should not be compared in terms of their absolute values which you've done here in your, I might say, quite elegantly done, hand graph. If you wished to take your elegant hand graph and compare it more appropriately to the new data, I might refer you to figure 1, appendix 2 of the 2002 report which I mentioned this morning. That is the graph which contains the original count data from the original four sources and would be a more appropriate comparison to what you've shown here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm through with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I need to have this marked as an exhibit, Your Honour, and it's going to be 4D something but I have no idea what and then perhaps we can somehow get it into the system.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC121, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's okay, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this analytical process, when you started the process, you started it with I think what might be characterised as a general understanding that there had been a fairly large number of Kosovo Albanian deaths. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, no. I started with the observation that there had been a lot of refugees. I didn't know how many deaths there were, and, in fact, even after I'd written my first report, it was not at all clear to me how many deaths there had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there was a time when you must have suspected there'd been a large number of deaths and then you started work on that and you applied statistical methods to arrive at a number which you believed might fairly reflect the number of deaths?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: There was such a point, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in your report at paragraph 1.3, that's in your original report to the OTP, you indicate that you arrived at an estimated number of 10.356.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you tell me the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says you arrived at an estimated number of 10.356. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first thing that strikes me about that is that seems to be a pretty precise number for an estimate.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, point estimates are of a point. When we interpret the number, we interpret it within a margin of error, as it's commonly called or, in more technical language, a confidence level. Throughout the report you'll find us analysing that number in terms of the confidence level, in terms of the error bands around it, both around this specific point estimate and in terms of the trends and patterns over time that we work with. That's why all the graphs in the appendices are accompanied by a similar graph or table which indicates the amount of error that we estimate to be associated with each point over time and space. For example, figure 12 in appendix 3 is one such graph. Figure 11 also -- in appendix 2. Figure 11 in appendix 2 of the same report is another such graph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was all interesting stuff. I don't think it had anything to do with my question. My question was: When you're doing an estimate, how do you arrive at such a precise number as 10.356? Why not 10.300 or 10.400? That sounds more like an estimate to me. That's the question I'd like to have answered.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Right. Okay. An estimate is not a number that we guess at, but, rather, a result that comes from fairly precise calculations. We report the exact results of the calculations, but we also report our uncertainty about the precision of those calculations. That's how statistics work. So if we have a number of people who were drawn from this room, if we select half the people in this room and I measure their weights, I can come up with an exact average of their weights, but if you ask me then to apply that average of weights to all the people in this room, I'll say: Well, the precise measure in the sample is, you know, 175 pounds, but it would be plus or minus 20 or 30 pounds. Okay. But there will be an exact point estimate of the average. Here there is an exact point estimate of the total deaths; however, no statistician would work with that point estimate as an exact figure. Instead, we would work with the confidence interval, the margin of error around that figure, and the margin of error is described in some detail in the appendix and how we calculated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I understand and I agree that 10.356 is not a number you just guessed at; it's a statistically derived number from other numbers you guessed at. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No. It's a statistically derived number based on the counts generated by our underlying sources and that -- to which we applied a commonly used technique called multiple systems estimation which produced this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And we'll talk about that a little later.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To show us and demonstrate to us how careful you were in arriving at this number of 10.356, you tell us in footnote 4 that all of the statistical programming connected to the estimation of the results was done independently by two analysts using separate computers and different software and their results were identical; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So these two independent analysts, not sharing, apparently, software or computers or what they were doing or anything else --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, we shared what we were doing, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You shared your data, for sure?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We shared the initial data and we shared the reasoning and the methods we applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And both of them came up with the number 10.356?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Within rounding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's what we just went through. I said how did you get that precise 10.356. Wouldn't it make sense for it to be 10.300 or 10.400? Now we get here where you say they come up with the exact same number --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We truncate it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, wait a minute. And I asked you if it's 10.356 and you said well, with rounding. Now, that makes no sense compared to the answer you gave me just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We truncate it to an integer. I'm sure we can recover the underlying fractions, if that's of interest to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to know how it would have affected your conclusions regarding killings if that number had come out, say, 20.742.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've just lost my earphones. There we go. It depends where the 20.742 were distributed. It might not have affected them at all; it might have changed them. It depends on how over time and space those 20.742 or whatever number you choose had been distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that there could have been no change or a profound change or something in between?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: There were a variety of other possible models which we report in appendix 2, some of which reached as high as 20.000 or more. I checked the patterns of all those models and none of them were substantively different from the model we had here. So if there were a much, much larger estimate and it were produced by the same techniques and methodologies used in this paper, I am skeptical that the results would have been different. If some radically different method were used, then you could potentially have used it -- you could have come up with a different result.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, then the obvious question becomes this: Why go through this very elaborate statistical process where two people are doing it independently of each other on different computers to arrive at this number 10.356 when it didn't make any difference; you could have just picked a number out of the air. Let's use the number 7.000 or let's use the number 12.000. It won't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Because that's not how science is done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I know that's not how science is done, but what you've just told me, it probably won't make any difference if that number is double what you found or half what you found.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm a bit baffled by the question. The question is: If you think you know the answer, can't you just make it up? Is that roughly what you've asked me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. What I'm asking you is, does this number have any significance to the analysis you performed by using it? I think you've just told me that it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The absolute number is not key to the analysis, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: What is key to the analysis is the distribution of that number across time and space, that's crucial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you can use any number as long as you distribute it the same?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, you don't distribute it. As long as that number is distributed the same. The analyst does not do the distribution. It's -- the structure of that sentence is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does the programme do the distribution?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No. The underlying data does the distribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the underlying data that gave you information about killings didn't include numbers anywhere near 10.356, did it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: It included 4.400.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's right. Are you aware that the current best number on Kosovar Albanian deaths is 4.200?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I think that may be the best number of documented deaths. Again, the point of this analysis is to include those that are not documented and, in all likelihood, will never be documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if one's taking into account all the bodies that have been found and identified plus all the people that are missing and have not shown up and you arrive at a number of 4200, you probably can't change much from that. And if that's the current number, if that's where we are today, then that's quite a ways from your number of 10.356 --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- and whether that's correct or not, I can't testify to, and I won't. I'm just asking you hypothetically if it's in that range, 4200, based on actual real-world figures, your statistically derived estimates are off by more than 150 per cent, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, you've embedded a fascinating hypothesis in the question, so let's go back and unpack that hypothesis and maybe we can get to the question. The hypothesis is that because people have only identified 4.200 bodies -- identified or claimed as missing, that that's all there are. Now, I've worked in a lot of countries where there have been mass atrocities from Peru to Guatemala to South Africa to East Timor, and in my experience identifying even this many is an astonishing accomplishment. It is very rare that very many people after a mass atrocity are identified, for dozens of reasons; among those, that the families don't see any point to report, there's not much -- they have little to gain by reporting anything, because all the witnesses have either fled or gone. Families may have left the country, what have you. There are many reasons, and each context has its own reason why relatively few people report. This said, as we discussed in the previous line of questioning, whether the number is 10.356 or 4200 turns out to make relatively little difference to the analysis being given in this report. Again, referring you to the graph, figure 1, appendix 2, the unadjusted graph with the raw data, we find the same pattern. So we can debate the validity of the statistical estimate of the total, but the underlying argument is the same whether or not you make the estimate or not. We made the estimate in order to correct for biases we were concerned about in the captured data.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you through?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Every answer you give raises new questions. I'm reasonably certain you have absolutely no data from Kosovo about the incidents that were reported. You're guessing about that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The incidents of reporting, do you mean the reporting rate?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, the reporting rate for people missing. I think you have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, actually, the reporting rate can never be analysed directly, sir. The reporting rate always has to be estimated, so you're correct, I never have direct evidence of the reporting rate, but neither does anyone else for any other country on earth because the only way the reporting rate can be analysed whether it's in Sweden, the best registry in the world, or in some very-difficult-to-document place is by estimating the total and then looking at your report totals and dividing into that estimated total. By it's nature, the reporting rate is unmeasurable in any direct sense, so you're right that I don't have that data but that's a word game.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You must know that one of the major issues in Kosovo today and yesterday and for the last several years has been the issue of missing persons and where are they and have they been found and every time a mass grave is found there's a major interest in identifying who was there. And people are constantly reporting: My Joe is still missing. Was he found there? And we're now eight or nine years down the road from that war. Don't you think we have a pretty good idea of how many people are missing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, let's see, I've been working in Guatemala for the last few months --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Guatemala. I'm talking about Kosovo. Don't you think we have a pretty good idea of how many people are missing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, you don't. Now, if the number 4200 just, hypothetically, is an accurate number, then the statistical analysis you did that put that number at 10.000 was off by 150 per cent, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, hypothetically, we can agree to anything, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We can agree to that, can't we?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: If we agree hypothetically that the number is 10.356, then my estimate was off by 0 per cent. I think that's a truism of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you can answer my question that hypothetically it's off by 150 per cent if the right number's around 4.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it a well-formed question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's a well-formed question but it's been answered because you've already told us that you don't think it will make a significant difference to the outcome of your work. But Mr. Ackerman is intent upon pursuing it and I'm not going to stop him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that causes one to wonder about the integrity of the rest of your statistical calculations. If you can be off by as much as 150 per cent in this statistical analysis, what if you're off by 150 per cent or 200 per cent or 800 per cent with regard to the rest of your work? It puts the rest of it in some question, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, I mean, we started off with a pretty bizarre hypothetical. If you divide by zero you can prove anything and that seems to me the structure of this questioning. I'm sorry. It doesn't strike me as very convincing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to change to a different subject now.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And we'll talk about something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to be clear. There may be a miscommunication here because of your understanding of what hypothetical means. Your thinking of hypothesis being posed and then carrying out an exercise to demonstrate whether or not they're right or not. But here, all that is being put to you is that it may actually be the fact that there were only 4.200. Now, you don't accept that, but assuming that is the case, I understand your answer is it doesn't make any difference -- or it's unlikely to make any difference to the outcome of what you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now we can move on, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were asked by the Prosecutor to assist in these matters to help determine the effects of KLA activity and NATO bombing on refugee movements and killings. That's basically what you were asked to do, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No -- I mean I was asked by the Prosecutor to do that after I'd written two reports and then I wrote one for them, but I began this work independently and carried it on for two years independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We already knew that. I'm getting to the point of when you started talking to the Prosecutor about what they asked you to do and that's what they asked you to do?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: They asked me to write up what I had presented in oral reports to them from my earlier work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you'd agree -- in fact, I wonder if you've ever heard of a statistician from the University of Wisconsin, now retired I think, John Steele. Do you know John Steele?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: It vaguely rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, a question almost anybody would ask if you were to pose what's going on here today to them just out of the blue, it would be: Isn't the best way to determine why people left, what caused people to leave, is just talk to them and ask them. Why are you using -- why are you using the rather inexact methods of statistics to try to answer a question that you could just ask the refugees about and get the specific answers to. I mean, it makes one wonder why you're here, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, lots of people do that. This is what I do. This is a different way of answering the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But somebody decided it was important for you to come and give this testimony instead of getting that information from the people who were there and who knew why they left and how long it took them to get to the border.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's a question for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, earlier in this case, Mr. Ackerman and his colleagues spent a great deal of time and effort trying to prevent the -- and successfully to some extent, the Trial Chamber from considering the answers to these particular questions as they might be posed. And in place of that, what I think we have is accounts from a number of people about what happened to them. And I expect - although, no doubt, I may be looking at it too simply - I expect that the Prosecution might try to link the statistical exercise to the statements that we've heard from witnesses. They may not be able to do so of course but I would be surprised if they weren't at least trying to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wonder, Dr. Ball, if you were told by the Prosecutor when asked to pursue this inquiry regarding what you and I have just been talking about, if you were told by them that there was a very significant concern regarding the truthfulness of refugee accounts and of what had happened in Kosovo and that's why you were asked to perform this kind of an analysis. Did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No. No one from the OTP has ever said any such thing to me. But now that you mention it, actually, that's something that former President Milosevic raised more or less continuously throughout his cross-examination. So that's certainly a place I've heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you've heard it other places, too. It's something, I think, you're quite familiar with, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: In terms of Albanian refugees being liars? That's pretty much come from former President Milosevic, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Don't you recall speaking at a conference for journalists sponsored by the crimes of war project in the year of 2000, May 5 and 6 of 2000, before you wrote your report in this case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And don't you remember that journalists there were expressing their concern that Kosovo refugees were relating stories that had been planted by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, you use journalists in the plural. There was a journalist there who told a story of a refugee who had misled her.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was Nancy Durham?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I believe so. I don't remember her in particular. And the discussion came up how my methods would handle people lying to us and I discussed it and I explained how we would deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Nancy Durham showed a film at that presentation and said that she decided to spill the beans about what was going on there at the border in terms of KLA influence on the stories of refugees, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's not how I recall her presentation. She presented it as having been misled by a single person and that's my recollection of the story. Perhaps you have spoken to her more recently, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't recall her talking in terms of spilling the beans?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you were -- you've talked today already about the methods you used. I think you used two when you were talking about the movement of refugees. The statistical analysis methods you used I think basically boils down to a data correlation process where you're correlating one body of data against another body of data to see what that shows you. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No. Data correlation is a very specific technique and I only used it for exploratory purposes here. That's not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. This morning at page 33, line 20, you were being asked by the Prosecutor about your November -- some changes to your November 2002 report, I think based upon some additional information you received regarding NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you indicated that you noted that the NATO air-strikes could be interpreted to have caused a reduction in killings of Kosovar Albanians --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, from 2002, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. And you say: "We interpreted that result as coincidental."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After you had explained that, saying you interpret it as coincidental. I don't think I need to read all of your words at this point.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I think you heard Judge Bonomy say: That might make some plausible sense without trying to make a judgement of it. It may be an action that because it engages the Serbs distracts them from killing Albanians that I can see. You heard Judge Bonomy say that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I didn't notice that you made any effort to correct him regarding his understanding of what you had said, did you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I didn't interpret it as a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But didn't you understand that he had misunderstood what you had said?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Well, it's a plausible interpretation. It's not the interpretation we drew in this report, but it could be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it is the case when you testified on the 2nd of May, 2003, in Milosevic about this same thing. What you said in a question from Mr. Nice regarding this data was this: "Most of the NATO air-strikes occur in late May and early June. We therefore think that although the statistical models will see that as a negative correlation because much later in the period there's much more air-strikes and fewer killings, more air strikes and fewer migrations." And then you say this: "We believe it's illogical to argue that air-strikes that occur in late May and early June can somehow be interpreted as having prevented or stopped killings that occurred weeks earlier."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's right. And this morning what I said was, we believe this is a coincidence. It should not be interpreted -- it should not be over interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, coincidence is probably a term of art that most of us don't understand. And I think you left Judge Bonomy with the belief that what you were saying is that the NATO air-strikes were reducing the death rates in Kosovo, and that's not what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, that's not what I was saying, and if I left that misinterpretation, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, in fact, you used this same statistical analysis that you used to arrive at the other things you're telling us to come up with these results which you then -- the only thing you can do when they are just obviously wrong is say: Well, okay, this is a coincidence. And because you can't now rely on them because they're just obviously wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is, with respect, engaging now in argument and not proper questions to an expert witness about his analysis and continuance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In our original report we cut off the analysis on May 11th precisely to avoid this, because we knew that after May 11th there were relatively few killings and relatively little migration. We did not want to continue the regression past that point, because we were concerned that the high level of bombings after that point would create such an artefact as you have expressed concerned about. We were asked to go ahead and extend the model. We did so. We then covered it in caveats, as you have noted, but when we are asked to do something, we do it, and then we interpret it as best we can. So if we're asked to do something which we feel is not perhaps the best appropriate scientific technique, we will nonetheless carry out the analysis but we will try the best we can to explain why the analysis is perhaps not the best statistical approach to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, is it -- you know, I'm just very confused, because it seems to me what you're saying is, if the model we use supports our hypothesis, then it's valid; if it doesn't support our hypothesis, then it's a coincidence and it's not valid. And it seems to me it either works or it doesn't work. So I think what you're proving here is that it doesn't work and that your data is flawed and your analysis is flawed and we shouldn't pay attention to it. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, and I must say your question is so long it would take quite a while to unpack all the reasons you're wrong --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: But I will, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You find it humorous, do you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No. I guess in California we smile a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And giggle?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: When models are constructed, we construct them carefully so that they are within the bounds that are appropriate for the piece of analysis necessary at hand. In particular, we are concerned about a phenomenon called outliers. Outliers are data points that are well outside the model but that may change the model in some radical way because they're part of a different pattern. What we judged and what we argued in this report is that there is a fundamental shift in the conduct of the conflict in mid-May, that in mid-May there are very few killings, very few migrations that occur after that point, after May 11th. There are, however, quite a few NATO bombings. In fact, the NATO air-strikes intensify throughout the late May/early June period. It would be in some sense tipping -- putting our thumb on the scale unfairly to include the period during which there are no NATO - excuse me - there are no killings or migration, but there are NATO air-strikes. It's not so much that the model is invalid but, rather, that it would overstate the impact of NATO's actions.
